speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a matter of urgent and pressing necessity dealing with the deadline for the report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution which is now sitting. In order to avoid any misunderstanding with respect to it, I have given notice of this motion both to the House leadership of the government and of the NDP. The motion, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), reads:
That the terms of reference of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution be hereby amended so that the deadline for the committee's report shall be February 10, 1981, instead of December 9, 1980, and that a message be sent to the Senate asking it to concur in this motion.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RENEGOTIATION OF NEW AUTO PACT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the Canadian deficit within the U.S.-Canada auto pact has reached a staggering $15 billion since 1965 and that 25,000 Canadians have lost their jobs within the industry and hundreds of thousands more in associated industries, creating widespread bankruptcies within this vital sector of our economy, and because the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), after having been so ineffective while the auto industry crumbled in front of his eyes, has seen fit to send a few officials to Washington merely to modify the auto pact, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brampton-George-town (Mr. McDermid):
That this House instruct the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to scrap the obsolete and inadequate auto pact so harmful to this country and attempt to replace it with a new package which would ensure that Canada receive its fair share of the assembly and production of fuel-efficient cars as well as parts and components manufactured in Canada for the so-called world car concept, and that during this transition period import quotas on offshore vehicles be imposed and an annual report of the over-all aspects of the auto industry in Canada be produced and tabled by the minister, as recommended in the Reisman report.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It concerns his announcement yesterday that the government will bankroll Imperial Oil, the richest oil company in Canada and a subsidiary of Exxon Corporation of the United States, the biggest oil company in the world, to the tune of $40 million for the Cold Lake project. 1975 to 1980, profits of something like $493 million last year and an increase in profits in the first nine months of 1980 of 56 per cent over last year, in view of all the money made by this rich company, why is it necessary for the Government of Canada to give the company an extra $40 million? speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT SUPPORT OF IMPERIAL OIL COLD LAKE PROJECT

Madam Speaker, there is a very simple reason. I agree that Imperial Oil is a wealthy and powerful company, but it has already spent $120 million on this particular project. For reasons which are well known, the government of Alberta has delayed over the last three years the approval of this project which, in our view, is a very important project if we are to achieve our goal of national autonomy or independence of oil supply.
Rather than see the team of 550 engineers and experts disbanded and this project shelved and abandoned indefinitely, it was felt it would be much better at this time, to ensure that the team would be kept together, to advance the money necessary over the next six months, shoved between the two governments preferably. Since I do not know whether Alberta is going to come up with its share, we said we would provide the full advance if they do not. If the project does proceed, the loan will be repaid with interest by Imperial Oil.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT SUPPORT OF IMPERIAL OIL COLD LAKE PROJECT

And if the project does not proceed, the government will throw away $40 million, I gather. I do not think the minister and hon. members opposite understand this.
I note that the whole basis of the national energy policy is to Canadianize the industry. What is the first act of Canadiani-zation, Madam Speaker? To give $40 million to Imperial Oil. Imperial Oil has stated that it considers the $38 per barrel oil price offered by the federal government too low to allow the project to proceed. If he wants the $40 million back, he will have to agree with Imperial Oil on the Cold Lake Project as to what the final price will be.

On the other hand, I have indeed spoken to the minister and he is ready, merely as an act of courtesy, to appear before the committee of which the hon. member is chairman or vice-chairman. He is ready to appear and provide explanations on the nature of the regulation-making powers liable to be involved in the legislation setting up a Post Office corporation.
Of course, we would like to have the bill referred to the committee as soon as possible this afternoon. Anyway, I confirm that the Postmaster General, as an act of courtesy and unofficially, without any formal reference to the relevant clause of the bill, is ready to appear before the committee chaired by the hon. member to provide some explanations.

Madam Speaker, I should like to get some clarification. The committee report was unanimous from members on all sides of this House and on both sides of the Senate. The committee asked that the regulation-making powers of this bill and of other bills, including broad regulation-making powers, be sent to the committee for study, for recommendation back to the House, and for amendment, if necessary, at second reading.
If I understand the government House leader correctly, is he saying that our committee would not have the authority to make amendments to the regulation-making authority granted in that bill, that that would remain exclusively with the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to raise a point of order arising out of the comments of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when he was reflecting upon the deliberations of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada earlier this after-
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
noon, wherein he accused opposition members of engaging in mischief.
In raising that question, I should like to refer to the fifth edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. On page 103, citation 316, sentence (e) indicates that a member while speaking must not:
impute bad motives or motives different from those acknowledged to a member;
Also sentence (f) goes on to indicate that a member while speaking must not:
make a personal charge against a member;
I do not think the Deputy Prime Minister was making any specific personal charges, even though two of us moved motions at that committee this morning, myself and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). But I suggest on a point of order that while he was speaking perhaps he did "impute bad motives or motives different from those acknowledged to a member".
As evidence of that I want to say that we moved those motions this morning for what I think are two very legitimate reasons. First, we believe that we need more time for the people and Canada to be heard on their constitution, and second, we need more time as members of that constitutional committee to study what in effect is a very controversial and detailed resolution before the committee. For those reasons we moved an amendment to recommend to Parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate, that consideration be given to extending the deadline to February 10. I think we had the right as a committee to make that recommendation, and we were not engaging in mischief of any sort or kind.
I want to say that we are doing and have done it because we have learned one thing, if nothing else, from the witnesses who have already appeared before us, that they need more time, that Canadians need more time. For example, this morning the Canadian Federation of Municipalities indicated that it needed more time to prepare, and asked for an extension of the deadline. Two days ago the Canadian Civil Liberties Association appeared before us. It indicated that it did not have a brief because it did not have time to prepare one and that we were dealing in this resolution with a very complicated and important charter of rights for the future of the country.
Also 1 have before me a letter which was addressed to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Joyal) and the Honourable Harry Hays, the co-chairmen of the Special Joint Committee on the constitution. It was signed by Marion Dewar who wrote to the co-chairmen on behalf of a number of organizations, and in part it reads as follows:
-respectfully requests that the Special Joint Committee on the constitution extend the final date for written submissions or requests to appear before the committee from Tuesday, November 25 to Wednesday, December 31, 1980.
Our discussions with Canadians in every part of Canada and from many sectors of Canadian life convince us that more Canadians want to be heard than the current timetable of your committee allows.
She is asking for an extension of the time on behalf of the many important organizations which signed their names to this letter. 1 want to know whether the Deputy Prime Minister

November 20, 1980
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
thinks we are being mischievous when we speak on behalf of the Anglican Church of Canada. Are we being mischievous when we say that we need more time because the Anglican Church is saying that we need more time? The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops is indicating that we need more time. Are we being mischievous when we move a motion on their behalf saying that we need more time? The Canada West Foundation is saying that we need more time, the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped is saying that we need more time. Is that being mischievous, Madam Speaker.
Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the National Indian Brotherhood, the Presbyterian Church of Canada and the National Anti-Poverty Organization are saying that we need more time. As a result we have moved a motion in the committee asking for an extension of the deadline to February 10.
The other reason we have done it is that we believe members of the committee need more time to study the resolution section by section. We need more time to study its impact on Canadians. We need more time to consider a number of amendments, which no doubt will be coming from all parties in the House, to the various sections contained in the resolution.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, to consider whether there has been an infringement of the rules by the Deputy Prime Minister, or whether indeed he was imputing motives to members of the opposition on that committee.
In closing, I want to say that I hope members opposite will consider revising the artificial deadline of December 9 because it means rushing through a very complicated constitutional package, one that might not stand the test of time, one that may be more divisive than helpful in the country, while we should be seeking a consensus, bringing Canadians together, and healing this country from coast to coast. If we can spend months studying the Bank Act in committee, and years in Parliament, then surely to goodness we can spend at least three months in a committee on the Constitution of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the point of order raised by the hon. member gives me an opportunity to make a comment on a recurring feature of the House proceedings which has been a cause of concern to me for some time, namely, the recurring practice of dealing in the House of Commons with matters which are before committees.
It is true that in my response to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) I did make reference to proceedings in the committee, which were introduced into the questioning by the Leader of the Opposition. Madam Speaker, both of us were out of order on that occasion. I propose at some future time to raise a point of order on this very point of order, to receive a ruling from the Chair as to whether it is appropriate for the
House of Commons to deal with matters on a daily basis, which have been referred to a standing or special committee by the House of Commons. There is a clear rule and a clear practice that no references, no debates and no discussion can take place on committee proceedings until a committee has reported to the House. That is a good, reasonable, and sensible rule. I believe-and I stated this quite clearly in my response to the Leader of the Opposition-I did breach that practice, to some extent.
I would like to reply to the member who raised the point of order, which objected to the word "mischievous". I must say that is a rather mild parliamentary attack. I could not find a milder word to describe what happened in the committee this morning. I regard the activities that were taking place quite worthy of the mild description of mischievous, in light of the fact there was a readiness stated by the government House leader to undertake negotiations with a view to dealing with the question of the deadline. He has already expressed his willingness to be flexible on this point. I believe it would have been useful for all members to await the result of these negotiations before launching into a procedure that took up a good deal of the committee's time. I hope in the future I will not breach the rules by discussing the proceedings of a committee of the House.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Such effrontery!

Madam Speaker, on the same point of order, 1 wish to say that on behalf of my colleagues 1 moved that motion this morning. It was a very straightforward motion asking that the length of time available to the committee be extended to February 6. It was then amended to February 10. Additionally, it was to extend the period of time for Canadians to submit written briefs or ask to be heard before the committee from November 25, which was the second arbitrary date imposed by the Liberal majority, to December 31.
With reference to what happened in the committee today, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) says that it was a mischievous action on the part of myself, I presume, because 1 was the person who moved that motion. An interesting point is that the Deputy Prime Minister has just said again that the House cannot interfere with the work of a committee and that a committee is to be master of its own proceedings. The hon. gentleman has used that argument, as has the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government House leader. But in refuting the arguments that were made by us in the committee, the Liberal members on that committee used the same tactic. The Deputy Prime Minister wants to use a double standard. The argument which the Liberal members used was that it was not for the committee to decide, that it was to go back to the House. They cannot have it both ways.
When it is in the House they say the committee should decide, and when it is in the committee they say the House should decide. The point is that they do not want anyone to
November 20, 1980

make any changes to their arbitrary date. That is the point. They do not want to change either the November 25 date or the December 9 date.
The Leader of the Government in the House says repeatedly that he will be flexible. There has been no indication of any flexibility on their part without strong pressure from this party to bring about changes. We saw that in connection with television. It was only after extreme pressure that they changed their position on that. They have not changed their minds even on the quorum-they do not want members of the official opposition to sit on the committee when the committee sits. In fact that committee can constitute itself without any member of the opposition there-with only government members there. Only government members need be there to hear evidence or to make decisions.
Consider the matter of the polls. They were not released. That committee is studying the constitutional amendments at this point in time. We know the government has polls paid for by the public which directly affect that discussion. But are they released? No. The Canadian people are not entitled to know. Yet today in the traditional Thursday question the government House leader said that the government wants to move forward on freedom of information legislation. But ministers will not release the polls.
Mauam Speaker, 1 have here a list of the witnesses who now want to appear before the committee. It is an extensive list. What happens in the committee, day after day, is that we get a list of witnesses who are to appear before the committee. The point that must be made is that the committee has not approved the list. Then, when we get a backlog it is we who are called mischievous. Not so. The list is in no way practical to the work of the committee. What 1 have asked for is not an indeterminate extension of the length of time. 1 asked for a two-month extension on behalf of Canadians-a two-month extension. 1 think that is very reasonable. It will enable not only the committee to do its work but, more important, it will enable Canadians who are asking to be heard, time to appear.
Is Mr. Borovoy of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association mischievous when he says to the committee that he needs more time? Is the Canadian Chamber of Commerce mischievous when its members say to us that they "could not prepare a brief prior to appearing here so what we are presenting to you is a policy position not directly related to the resolution?" Is the Federation of Canadian Municipalities mischievous when it asks for time to hold a board meeting in order that they might bring-

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, obviously the hon. member's attitude this morning in committee was perhaps honest, but it is not the most honest we have ever seen. By far it is not the most honest attitude we might have expected.
The following facts should be recalled briefly. First, the hon. member knew from the answers I gave yesterday in the House to the NDP leader and the Progressive Conservative leader that I intended to meet with the House leaders. Second, even though he knew of this ensuing discussion between House leaders on the length of the committee proceedings, he decided, purely for reasons of political expediency, to introduce a motion in committee asking for an extension of the deadline, knowing full well that the House of Commons, the Senate, the institution of Parliament gave a specific mandate to the committee to consider the matter and report back by December 9. So, when the hon. member refers to the principle that the committee is master of its own procedure only when it is convenient for us, I must respectfully tell him that he is totally wrong. Of course, the committee is master of its own procedure, but within the terms of reference it has been given by the House and, in this case, by the Senate. These terms of reference make it very clear that there is a time limit, namely, December 9. Therefore, the committee knows that its time is limited and that if the House wants to grant an extension, this decision must be made by the representatives of all parties, and it also knows that the House leaders will meet to discuss the matter and that we have already indicated our wish to be flexible, as the Prime Minister said himself last week, and as I said yesterday and again today. In spite of all this, the committee wasted two hours of its time this morning and a group of ladies were kept waiting in a shameful and unacceptable manner, and they are still waiting because the members of the committee are now in the House wasting time by raising procedural questions on this subject. In spite of all this, we heard today a motion under Standing Order 43, a procedure which is much abused, which motion was moved by my colleague, the Progressive Conservative House leader, even though he is well aware that we shall be meeting at five o'clock this afternoon to discuss this matter in good faith, and I intend to show him the type of flexibility we have been talking about. Once again, I do not bear him any grudge for this, but I would still like to note that he should know that we are going to discuss this matter this afternoon. And yet he thought it proper to use Standing Order 43 to repeat before the House the same type of question which was asked in the committee.
I wonder whether the Progressive Conservative Party really wants to take advantage of the flexibility that we are willing to show. I give them the benefit of the doubt, and the meeting at five o'clock will still be held and it may be followed by other

November 20, 1980
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
meetings. It will depend on the pace of the negotiations and the discussions. However, I must say that the position taken by the Progressive Conservative Party to date seems rather ambiguous to me.
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) is also wrong when he tells us that we gave no indication of flexibility as to the date for the report of the committee. I want to state publicly that, as a matter of fact, and I say it again because I have already said it publicly, I told them in early October that this matter could be discussed. Yesterday, my colleague was going around with the minutes of the meetings we had, and 1 hope he will refer to them. I call upon my learned colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to bear witness to that. However, I am convinced that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is candid enough not to deny obvious facts. I also told them that the form of the debate in the third stage could be discussed, and I invited them to do this systematically. In fact, they have always refused to discuss it until now.
As recently as last week I reminded my learned colleague from Nepean-Carleton that we were prepared to reconsider the date and form of the committee report, as well as the length of the debate at the third stage. He took my request under advisement and will hold consultations, and I hope that this afternoon we shall finally be able, a month and a half after my request, to discuss the deadline openly, honestly, without any of the tactics such as the one we witnessed this morning in committee and this afternoon during proceedings under Standing Order 43.
Madam Speaker, may I refer you to paragraph 659 of Beauchesne's, at page 205, which bears out the Deputy Prime Minister regarding the procedure and says very clearly that it is irregular to comment on what is going on in the proceedings of a committee when there is no report before the House. Here is what clause (1) says:
(1)	Until the report and the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence have been laid upon the Table, it is irregular to refer to them in debate, or to put questions in reference to the proceedings of the committee.
(2)	When the report and the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence are before the House, they may be debated at length but members are not permitted to discuss the conduct or language of members of the committee, except so far as it appears on the tabled report.
(3)	If alleged irregular proceedings take place in committee but are not referred to in the report that the committee presented to the House, then it is not competent for the House to go beyond that report to debate this matter.
Madam Speaker, nothing can be clearer and more precise. It is entirely irregular to ask questions and have a discussion about what happened in committee until we receive a report from that committee. And in the future, I shall respectfully point out that we on this side of the House shall insist, out of respect for this institution, on having the rules enforced.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very interested in the insistence now of the government House leader on this matter. Perhaps some intimidation of the Chair is intended, but I would hope not. I want my friend to know that if he is talking about a limitation of time as the price for answering the request of the organizations of the people of Canada then, having had to submit to closure a little while ago, I am not disposed to submit to closure of another kind as the price for something else.
1 would be a stupid man if 1 agreed to give this government, in advance, a blank cheque with respect to what a committee may report at some future time and with respect to what the government may do with that report at a future time. If that is what they want, they are not going to get it. It is that simple. If my friend is prepared-

-and indeed, by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen)-making statements, not a press release- and by the Deputy Prime Minister today in first of all labelling as mischievous the activity of members of Parliament designed to ensure that the people of Canada are heard on the Constitution of Canada and, secondly, in his very presumptuous behaviour in lecturing you on how you should do your job, and to lecture me as to how 1 should do mine.

November 20, 1980
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
conducted himself so far. I do not want to be distracted by the government House leader's interventions however.
The point I want to make is that in this House of Commons public business can get done only when certain standards of trust are accepted and established, and the behaviour of the government on this matter very seriously jeopardizes that atmosphere of trust that is essential to this House making progress on any matter at all.
Let me deal with one or two of the matters that have been raised, Madam Speaker. First of all, 1 think it highly inappropriate of the Deputy Prime Minister, who has now abandoned the House-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-the Deputy Prime Minister whose comments caused this question of privilege, who intervened and then left the House-I think it highly improper that he should suggest to you, Madam Speaker, what matters and questions you should find in order, after you have clearly found those matters and questions to be in order. It is no part of his duty to tell you how to do your job.
Second, the House will recall that the government House leader in the other place quite explicitly indicated in answers to questions in that other place that it would be within the capacity of the joint committee to make the request to both Houses to change the reporting date of the committee. That was an undertaking, a statement of the policy of the Government of Canada, made in response to a question, by a minister of the Government of Canada, the House leader of the government in the other place. That was the answer by the government spokesman in the Senate on which the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville were acting today when they sought to follow the suggestion made by a representative of the Government of Canada to seek to have the committee itself act to extend its time.
Now let me deal, if I might, with a point that was made by the Acting Prime Minister before he left the House. He suggested that the questions that were raised by myself and allowed by the Chair were out of order. My questions were designed to ask the policy of the Government of Canada on this question, and 1 would find it quite strange if it were improper, if it were ruled by the Chair that the fact that a particular draft resolution on the Constitution of Canada is before a joint committee of this House and the other place, that that fact alone would prevent this Parliament or, indeed, the Senate of Canada, from asking questions as to the policy of the Government of Canada with regard to the Constitution of Canada. That is the position that has been put forward by the government. It is a wholly untenable and an unacceptable position.
The reason we are asking, for the policy of the government is that it has become so clear that the Liberal members on that committee are operating clearly as agents of the government rather than simply as members of this Parliament and of the
Senate of Canada. They are operating on instructions to the point that some members are even reading briefs that are prepared by consultants associated with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien)-with the minister whose name is on the bottom of the draft resolution. We have here a situation where the policy of the government must be known because the policy of the government is dictating the behaviour of the Liberal members on that committee.
What we have here-the government House leader, who has been sat down by you, Madam Speaker, for his interventions earlier, is shouting across the floor. He may have an opportunity later to speak. The very clear point with which we are dealing here is that for a series of days the Government of Canada has been seeking some soft way to impose a new kind of closure upon the debate by the Parliament of Canada-by the House of Commons and the Senate-to impose a soft kind of closure upon discussion by representatives of the people of Canada of the Constitution of Canada. He knows he was wrong in imposing closure, the formal rule of closure, on this House in a circumstance where more government members had spoken than members of the official opposition. He knows that was wrong. What he is going to do now is to seek other means-seek closure by some other name. The goal is the same-the goal of the government-and that goal is to limit debate by Canadians of their constitution. To limit that debate, wherever it occurs, whether in the committee or here, or in the public at large-that is their goal. That is why they resisted television; that is why they resisted radio. That is what their secret document said. That is why they imposed closure on this House.
Their goal is to try to keep the people of Canada in ignorance about the contents of the constitutional proposal. They are worried that when groups such as the Canadian Association for Adult Education, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Anglican Church of Canada, and Le regroupement pour les droits politiques du Quebec-they are concerned that when these groups come to testify before the joint committee, Canadians will learn just how full of fault and danger this particular measure is. So they are trying to find some excuse to cut off debate. They did it with closure once in this House, and now, knowing that closure is politically unpopular, they are trying to find a softer way to limit debate.
Today, the Deputy Prime Minister referred to groups such as the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Canada West Foundation, the National Indian Brotherhood, the Presbyterian Church of Canada and a number of others, as mischievous. I suggest that rather than insulting those groups of Canadians who want to have their views heard on the Constitution of Canada, the Government of Canada should be hearing those Canadians and should be allowing the people of Canada to hear the views expressed by their various organizations and by interested individuals in the Canadian populous rather than resorting to various techniques designed to limit debate in committee and designed to impose a quiet form of
November 20, 1980

closure upon the ability of the people of Canada to have their views heard on their constitution.

I assume we will be discussing that this afternoon when we meet at five o'clock, and I hope we can have a pleasant meeting. Perhaps the government House leader, with his sometime courtesy, will have some coffee and tea available and we can have a friendly discussion.

My leader yesterday was asking for an extension of time for the committee on its own. 1 read one sentence to emphasize the point, which is found at page 4848 of yesterday's Hansard. The hon. member for Oshawa said:
What I would like clear from the government House leader is that he is not considering a trade-off.
It may well be that he is, but the hon. member for Oshawa was very clear yesterday that he was asking for an extension of time because of the importance of the issue. speechtext:
This point of order was raised on a matter protesting the fact that the hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was imputing bad motives by using the word "mischievous" to qualify some of the motions which have been made by some members of Parliament. That was the beginning of it. He strayed very far from the first indication of what that point of order was all about, but 1 will come to that later.
I have to say that I did not feel the Deputy Prime Minister was imputing bad motives in using that expression, nor was he making the kind of charge which it is customary to prohibit in this House. It is true the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) did quote from Beauchesne, but as a matter of
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
fact I think the interpretation of these conditions has to be much more generous on both sides.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville has explained the kind of "mischief', if I may use that word because I do not dare use another word, to describe what he was up to in the committee. I suppose the House is better for having been more informed about what took place. I gave the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville quite a lot of latitude to expose his point of order. I suppose that disposes of this grievance, because that is what it is; it is not a question of privilege.
My main concern though is a number of references which have been made to committee proceedings. This whole thing was prompted by a question from the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). He has explained that he was inquiring about a matter of policy, and he was not referring directly to the actual proceedings of the committee. I must say that I nearly jumped to my feet when I heard him formulate his question, and then decided against doing that, probably because I was sure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would never want to do anything against the rules of this House; and I do not think that he has. But then in the response made by the Deputy Prime Minister there was a reference made to committee proceedings. The Deputy Prime Minister himself agreed that he had perhaps breached the rules by making that kind of reference.
I think the rule has been breached quite a number of times subsequently during the course of the debate this afternoon. 1 will have all of these interventions examined so as to determine the number of times when I feel members have come very close to debating proceedings of committees.
The hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) quoted the rule, which is quite clear, so I will not repeat it. But it is right here in Erskine May where it is very clear that this House should not be referring to proceedings of committees.
1 have just one more point. I want to remind hon. members that they should not refer to committees, even obliquely, in the House. I will read all of the speeches that have been made this afternoon in order to make it somewhat easier for me to spot circumstances when members are really referring to proceedings of committees. The Chair has some difficulty, because one has to listen to the end of one sentence and then to a second sentence to know whether it is really a breach of the rule. That is why sometimes I have to be a bit lenient about that.
I just want to remind the hon. Leader of the Opposition that when members raise points of order or try to help me to interpret the rules of this House, I am grateful for that kind of contribution, and I do not consider that I am being lectured when members do that, no matter on which side of the House a member sits. It is helpful to the Chair when members try to concentrate on the point of procedure being raised. It is helpful if they bring forward arguments to enlighten the Chair and so help the Chair to make a ruling. Therefore I do not consider that I am being lectured to when that happens. As a matter of fact, 1 welcome it. I think it would be wise to put an end to this debate this afternoon. The exchange that has taken place will,

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, October 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-42, to establish the Canada Post Corporation, to repeal the Post Office Act and other related acts and to make related amendments to other acts, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Madam Speaker, in the context of the preceding hour and a quarter I think I have to deal with some of that as part of my remaining 16 minutes. However, I was interested that the parliamentary secretary mentioned that there were members of the postal union in our gallery today. I too welcome them on behalf of the members of this party.
I would like to point out to the members of the union who sit in the gallery that I have been waiting anxiously for over three weeks to finish the speech I started. I would like to point out to members of this House that it is the government which controls the order of business. It is the government which has decided not to debate the postal bill for the last three weeks. It was in fact the government which decided not to bring this bill forward in May, and it is the government which will probably leave this chamber, talk to the news media and accuse us of breaking agreements and talking out bills. That was my experience when I began this speech three weeks ago.
The tone of the press articles related to my attempt to deal with the postal bill had two misinterpretations of what I was attempting to do in this chamber. The first was that I was using the time of the House to deal with the issue of closure, and I was not. I made no deliberate attempt to talk out the bill. I, like any member of this chamber, am entitled to speak
It should be clear to the Canadian public, after the last few days of broadcasting of that committee, that it is in fact the members of the Liberal party, the government party, who control the debate in committees. It should be much more clear to the Canadian public that the rules of this House provide for standing committees to be dominated in their voting strength by members on the government side. It should be clear to members of the House and to Canadians generally that in such a situation it is possible for prime ministers and cabinet ministers to put considerable pressure on members of standing committees to use up the time in asking non-incisive questions and voting as instructed.
Once this House completes second reading of the postal bill, the bill moves to committee where there will be no television, no broadcasting, and no opportunity for members of the opposition to bring to the attention of the Canadian public what may be wrong with the bill. In the House we have a simple tool, that is, television in the House and the potential for radio broadcasting, which gives us as the representatives of the people the opportunity to make Canadians aware of what we perceive to be the positive as well as the negative features of legislation. It is in that context that I wish to continue my remarks for the ten minutes that I have left. We do not seek to delay, we take our responsibility seriously and we seek to improve legislation so as to create a better world for Canadians within the context of pieces of legislation.
Since I began working on this speech three weeks ago 1 have learned a lot. I am a relatively new member of this House and I have the opportunity of watching how this government functions. Today we have had closure imposed on the constitutional committee; we were denied the opportunity to call witnesses and to continue discussions in committee beyond December 9, in spite of the fact that all the witnesses who have appeared before that committee indicated extreme dissatisfaction with the bill. When the postal bill moves to committee, will we face the same kind of closure? If the government is consistent, which I believe it is, then we will face that kind of closure. Ministers will use their majority to decide what amendments to accept, what amendments to reject and what witnesses to hear, and we will end up, as a consequence of a

November 20, 1980

process of that kind, with legislation which is not as good as it could be and should be.
1 said to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) the other evening that a government which deals with a free people, when it seeks to govern without the support, without the help of those who are to be governed, invites revolution and imperils the will of the people affected to work together and, in the case of the constitution, perhaps even the will to survive as a nation. The protection that free people have is a free forum, a Parliament to which people elect their representatives and where the procedures are such that those who are elected are entitled to speak out on behalf of those whom they represent.
It is in that context that the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) began his remarks on this bill. I want to remind everyone that he began those remarks by telling us that some ten years ago a Liberal government brought changes to the Post Office without adequate discussion and consultation. The consequence of that action was a postal service which Canadians have judged not to have been satisfactory in this decade.
As we look at the constitutional bill and as we look at the budget we see the mistakes of ten years ago being repeated, namely, lack of consultation, lack of common sense, lack of respect for the process of discussion and dialogue. Not only does this imperil the postal delivery service but, in my view, it imperils a nation in political terms and in economic terms. The government may seek to blame the opposition for delaying this bill and they will succeed in the short term, but those who work in the Post Office and those who represent them here today in our galleries might be wise to listen to the debate and to decide for themselves whether the points which we raise in the process of the debate should be listened to. I would feel somewhat better had the Postmaster General been present to hear any part of my remarks. I hope a person on his staff will at least read them to him.
In the postal bill before us, at page 4 in clause 5(2), we have a provision which looks innocuous. This reminds me of the charter of rights. When Canadians first saw it, it looked good, it looked innocuous. As we hear testimony in the constitutional committee, we find it to be dangerous, badly worded, and likely to change the very nature of this country in some unpleasant ways. That is what we find when we examine it word by word.
If we look at just the four simple objectives of this new Crown corporation, what do we find? Clause 5(2)(a) reads:
the desirability of improving and extending its products and services in the light of developments in the field of communications;
That sounds as if we wanted a better Post Office, and who could object to that? But that objective for the Crown corporation, coupled with what we find in later clauses-the regulatory powers which I am sure the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) will address more articulately than I can-will result in the creation of a new Crown corporation to run our Post Office, a Crown corporation with the power of massive intrusion into the private sector in this country. I ask the Postmaster General: is he handing the board of directors and the president the tools to throw every courier
Canada Post Corporation Act
service in this country out of business? The minister may say he does not intend to do that, but I ask him whether or not these words will allow him to do that, because, if they do, they must be changed.
Canadians do not want the Post Office running more of our economy. They want a Post Office running an efficient mail service, a Post Office which is humane to its employees, a Post Office which brings work satisfaction and which helps the economy of this nation by providing an efficient service. Why does the minister seek, in the objectives of this corporation, greater intrusion into our lives, an intrusion which is not sanctioned by Parliament on a piece by piece basis but which will be sanctioned by a president and a small board of directors?
What does clause 5(2)(b) indicate to us? It indicates:
-the need to conduct its operations on a self-sustaining financial basis while providing a standard of service that will meet the needs of the people of Canada;
We would like a post office which provides a good and efficient service and pays for itself. We must be very careful of words drafted by the government opposite, because it also hands that small group of people, that small board of directors appointed by the government, the power to tax Canadians. If it is to be self-sustaining, they get to levy the charge; no one is allowed to intrude on their area of jurisdiction and Parliament has no control over it.
On October 28 we sat in the House of Commons and listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) take another Crown corporation called Petro-Canada and give its board of directors the power to tax Canadians without representation. That is what he did with that Crown corporation, that is what he wants to do with the postal bill. That gradual, creeping tendency to hand over taxation powers to appointed people runs counter to our principle that people should be elected and accountable to the voters of this country when they have the right to tax those voters.
The third objective contained in clause 5(2) reads as follows:
(c)	the desirability of utilizing the human resources of the corporation in a manner that will both attain the objects of the corporation and ensure the commitment and dedication of its employees to the attainment of those objects-
Surely that is a motherhood clause which we hope any business enterprise would hold dear. But do they couple it anywhere in this legislation with the requirement for a comprehensive audit which will make it clear to government and to Canadians that in fact that is occurring? I suggest that they do not. They state it as a goal, but the machinery to protect the employees of the Post Office is lacking.
Now I come to the last objective which is a strange one in the context of the preceding three. It reads:
(d)	the need to maintain a corporate identity program approved by the governor in council that reflects the role of the corporation as an institution of the Government of Canada.
In light of the PetroCan experience, I cannot help wondering whether that corporate identity will be invented in New York City rather than in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, every Thursday for the past three weeks I have risen in my place, at the beginning of orders of the day, to make a request of the government House leader regarding House business. In each instance I have referred him to the report of the Standing Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. The fourth report of the committee was tabled by me in the House of Commons last July. It is before the House at the present time for study by hon. members and by the Canadian people.
The request I made of the government House leader related to Bill C-42 to create a Crown corporation for the Canada Post Office. I asked him whether he would accede to the request made unanimously by the members of the standing joint committee, of which I am one of the joint chairmen, that the government send the regulation-making powers contained in Bill C-42 to our committee for study after second reading. At the present time the government's intention is to send the whole bill to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates for study.
My request to the minister was that those portions dealing with regulation-making authority, which would give the government incredibly broad power to make regulations in the dark of night, without consultation with Parliament, should be sent to our committee for scrutiny, for amendment if necessary, and for recommendations to the House of Commons as to whether or not they should be restricted in some way.
An hour ago the government House leader refused that request. He said that he was not prepared to accede to the request of the standing joint committee. Instead he offered that the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) would appear as a
matter of courtesy before the committee, but that the whole of the substance of the bill would go to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. That statement is unacceptable to me, and I believe it would be unacceptable to the members of the standing committee who have asked me to make this request of the government.
Earlier this afternoon the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette) indicated that he felt there was an agreement or a disposition on the part of members of Parliament to put this legislation through today. I should like to indicate, as forcefully as I can, that, as the parliamentary secretary later recognized, there is no undertaking on the part of my party that this bill should be put through this afternoon. If the government is not prepared to come to its senses and to allow expert scrutiny of those regulation-making powers, then there are very dangerous powers in the bill which must be debated on the floor of the House of Commons.
I want to make an offer right now-and I will put it as directly as I can to the Postmaster General and the government House leader-if they want this bill through today, they will get it through today if they accede to the request I made earlier this afternoon on behalf of the standing joint committee. If they agree to send those regulation-making powers to our committee, then the members of the official opposition are prepared to accept the bill and allow it through today. But we would ask that all regulation-making authority, including the ability to set postal rates by the Post Office, be sent to the standing joint committee and that that committee have the power refused it earlier today by the government House leader to make amendments to those provisions, if necessary.
Why is it necessary? Why are the members of the standing joint committee concerned about this? Why do they feel that it is a matter of some urgency? I should like to refer the House to paragraph 67 of the committee report which deals with some of the threats that are created when the government asks for a broad regulation-making power which gives it the authority to make regulations in the dark of night without having to come back to Parliament. The paragraph reads as follows:
Far too many statutes contain little or no indication of legislative policy and are neutral documents the object of which is merely to confer powers on the executive to act in certain vaguely defined fields. Moreover, these powers are granted in very broad terms so that little or no detail is given as to the content or type of delegated legislation that can be made. It is too easy to dismiss this type of statute as "skeletal"; the problem is more serious than that. Even a skeletal statute can be fairly specific about the powers it grants and what can be done under them. To many Canadian statutes are not specific in that way.
Further, in paragraph 69, the committee goes on to say:
Your committee is convinced that the so-called principles used by the Department of Justice to justify the inordinate breadth with which powers are invested after passage are simply rationalizations for practices of great convenience to administrators but subversive of parliamentary supremacy over the law. The true practice and principle is simply this: the intentions of Parliament in delegating powers and the scope of the delegation should be beyond all doubt and clearly limited.
November 20, 1980

Paragraph 70 reads as follows:
Insufficient attention is paid to enabling clauses in bills before Parliament. They should be the subject of searching scrutiny during the committee stage. The Regulatory Review Committee-
That is the change in name we are asking be given to our committee.
-is well placed to undertake such scrutiny as it sees week by week the consequences of the powers so readily granted by Parliament in the past. Your committee, therefore, further recommends that the Regulatory Review Committee be charged with the duty and responsibility of examining and reporting upon all powers in bills to make subordinate law or to issue, make or establish other instruments. Its reports should be made to the appropriate standing committees of the Houses having the committee stages of the bills.
What could be a more reasonable request on behalf of the standing committee? That is the request that the members on this side of the House are making to the government today. We would expect some indication from the government as to whether it is willing to accede to that request.
Mr. Speaker, what is there in the bill itself that would give Canadians concern about the regulation-making authority? Members on this side of the House have indicated on numerous occasions in the past that we support the concept of a Crown corporation. We want to see measures taken which will improve the efficiency of the Post Office and make it so that Canadians have a guarantee that when they put a letter in the mail it will be delivered promptly and efficiently. We are convinced the organizational structure of a Crown corporation is one that could go some way toward making improvements, but there are serious flaws in this bill which give inordinate power to the government to operate by regulation.
What am I referring to, Mr. Speaker? I would bring to the attention of the House the regulation-making powers in the bill which make it clear that the Post Office will have the right and the responsibility to make regulations, including about 14 or 15 different regulation-making powers mentioned in here. It includes giving it the power to define, for the purposes of the act, what constitutes a letter. Why is that significant? If you look under the definition section on page two of the bill the government defines the phrase "mail conveyance" as follows:
"mail conveyance" means any physical, electronic, optical or other means used to transmit mail;
And the bill defines "transmit" as follows:
"transmit" means to send from one place to another by any physical, electronic, optical or other means;
The government then is giving the Post Office, by regulation, the right to define what constitutes a letter, including electronic mail, messages sent electronically or optically, not just in the way in which we have conventionally seen mail in the past-something that is physical which you can hold in your hand. When you couple that power to make regulations to sweep in the telecommunications industry of Canada under the ambit of the Post Office, and you couple that with the power of the Post Office, which is included in this bill, to declare a monopoly over the delivery of all mail in Canada, you can see that the government, by regulation, could be giving the Post Office the right to put the telecommunications industry in Canada out of business. This will happen unless it
Canada Post Corporation Act
is prepared to go along with conditions set by the Post Office, as one of the interested players. That would be bad enough if it were simply in the private sector, if it were in areas currently regulated by federal statute. But when you take a look at provisions in this bill you discover that this bill extends the power of the government beyond what it has ever been in the past.
Section 3 of the bill, under Application, reads:
This act is binding on Her Majesty in Right of Canada or a province and on any agent thereof.
What does this mean? It means that telephone companies owned by provincial governments are suddenly to be swept under the regulation-making power of the Post Office and of the ability of the Post Office, by regulation, to define their right to have a monopoly in this area. It may seem absurd for us to think that the Post Office would seriously want, in the dark of the night, to exercise this authority. It may be that members of the House would feel that it is simply an oversight on the part of the government that this was included in here.
I would refer members to the Clyne commission report, which was produced last year. It is entitled "Communications in Canada" and it looked at the predecessor bill, C-27. It reads as follows:
The federal government should consider the introduction of amendments to Bill C-27 (for the creation of a Post Office corporation) with a view to clarifying the role of the corporation in the telecommunications structure as a whole, which must continue to include the private telecommunications carriers.
It points out precisely the concerns which 1 have raised this afternoon. These were concerns which existed in the predecessor bill. It was not just a case of sloppiness, that the drafters of the bill were not aware of the scope of the regulation-making power being given to the government in this bill. The Clyne commission pointed this out a year ago and asked that those provisions be redrafted in a very specific way to ensure that monopoly power could not be extended over telecommunications. Yet Bill C-42, before the House today, has not been changed to correspond with what the Clyne commission report recommended.
Members of the government may say it is silly to suggest they would even want to sweep these people in under their monopoly. And maybe they do not want that. We do not know; there has been no discussion in the House so far.
It is worth while to look at a document put out by the Post Office. We ask ourselves what is the effect of competition on the Post Office. Is the Post Office interested in getting into the electronic mail field? I should make it clear that we on this side of the House do not have objections to the Post Office getting into the field of electronic mail, as a competitor, but we object to them sweeping their monopoly powers over the whole of the industry to put their competitors out of business. Is that something which we should be concerned about?
Mr. Speaker, if we look at a document entitled "Considerations which affect the choice or organization structure for the Canada Post Office", which was produced by the previous Postmaster General in August, 1978, we find appendix C of the report entitled "Impact of Alternative Communications

November 20, 1980
Canada Post Corporation Act
Methods and Systems". It deals with potential competition to the Post Office under the titles of telephone, data transmission, couriers, facsimile, word processing, and funds transfer. In the summary it points out:
The information funds transfer market-excluding mail and telephone-could be handling the following millions of letter equivalents by 1995:
It breaks it down to a grand total of 7,980 million letter equivalents. What this means is that the Post Office is projecting itself that by 1995 the telecommunications industry of Canada will be moving the equivalent of almost eight billion one-page letters. Those pressures will indeed be there upon the Post Office to extend its monopoly powers, and I think that Canadians have a right to be concerned. We should ask ourselves: would this also include companies like Bell Telephone? Could they be put out of business by what the Post Office is doing? On a cursory reading of the legislation before the House today, the answer is that probably they could. The Post Office, through its regulation-making authority, its power to define what constitutes a letter, could even define telephone conversations as letters. That power is totally unrestricted in the bill. If the minister wants to say that is not what they intend to do, then my response to him is: let us straighten up the language in this bill to make sure that it cannot be done.
The minister should be aware of the fact that the telephone system in Canada is digitizing and packetizing-if you will pardon the jargon-telephone conversations. What this means is that bits of information are turned into digital forms of communication similar to what is used for computers. They are moved into the packet-switching networks which cross this country, and they are moved along with electronic mail with computer communications in exactly the same way as electronic mail and other forms of electronic telecommunication exchanges. Oral communications over the telephone and electronic mail conveyed through packet-switching networks are virtually indistinguishable. There is no doubt in my mind that this bill would give the authority to the Post Office to sweep even provincially-owned telephone companies under the powers of its monopoly.
The issue is that if what the government is saying is that this is not its intention, and ministers have never said what their intention is in the field of electronic mail, to get involved in electronic mail except as a competitor, then let us word the bill so that they do not have the power, by regulation, without coming back to Parliament, to extend the monopoly powers of the Post Office in the telecommunications field.
If the government is saying that it wants to extend the powers of telecommunications so that there is a monopoly in the field, then it has the responsibility to come to Parliament and ask for that particular authority up front, as opposed to doing it by dark of night, by regulation. We are talking about a multibillion dollar industry upon which thousands of jobs in Canada rely, and about communications between individual Canadians and between businesses in this country. Surely Canadians and surely this Parliament have a right to expect
that legislation put before Parliament should be worded in such a way that the intentions of the Post Office are made clear and that the Post Office is not asking for a blank cheque to extend its monopoly to whatever area it chooses.
This issue is vital to Canadians. I cannot think of a single bill before Parliament at this time in which the government is asking for broader more unfettered regulation-making authority than in the case of this bill.
It is essential that the government agree with the proposition which 1 proposed in the course of my remarks. If it is prepared to reverse what the government House leader said earlier, and send those regulation-making powers, including the power to set rates-which would be done by regulation with only the right of appeal to the Canadian Transport Commission-to the standing joint committee, then the members on this side would be prepared to let the bill go through tonight. But if the government continues to ask for carte blanche authority and refuses the unanimous request of the standing joint committee that this sort of action should be taken, then we would have the obligation to continue to raise these matters on the floor of the House.
I have some other concerns with regard to this bill which I would like to touch upon very briefly in the time that is still available to me. One thought which members of Parliament should have when looking at this whole issue of a Crown corporation is what is the government doing in terms of the powers it is giving to the Postmaster General and the governor in council.
Hon. members should also think about how the government's plans correspond with the stated policy of the government with regard to Crown corporations. Hon. members will remember that in the last Parliament our government tabled a Crown corporation bill which dealt with a number of these areas. That bill would have given the government the power to issue directives in the national interest to Crown corporations, but those directives would be public and would be tabled in the House of Commons within 15 days of their being issued.
This bill, however, gives that power to an individual minister or to the governor in council to be used either openly or secretly. This bill gives the Postmaster General the power to give directives secretly to the Post Office. In our Crown corporations legislation we said that it was essential that the boards of Crown corporations operating on a commercial basis be given the authority to do their jobs. If there are good boards, then let them run their corporations.
Unlike the Crown corporation legislation which may be brought forward in the course of the next two weeks by this government, and the Prime Minister has claimed parentage of that bill-I am glad to give him that parentage as long as I am at least called an uncle when the legislation comes back before the House-we believe it is essential that the board of directors of Crown corporations be given the authority to appoint vice-presidents. This legislation says that any appointments of vice-presidents must be confirmed by the governor in council. One can think of the opportunities of patronage which are available in such a bill.
November 20, 1980

Such appointments would also allow the government to monkey around with the day to day affairs of a corporation just as secret directive powers would give it the same authority. This bill also says that the governor in council, not the board of the new Crown corporation, will have the authority to set the salary scales for vice-presidents of the Crown corporation. Here again is another instance of where there is a collision between these two principles and where the government wants to have political hands on the functioning of the Post Office. 1 believe that should be changed.
There is another matter which should be of concern to Canadians. 1 do not know whether the Postmaster General has had an opportunity to see the article which appeared in Monday's edition of the "Trudeau Star", an authoritative source for the Liberal party. The lead editorial on Monday evening dealt with the issue of Bill C-42. It expressed alarm that if this bill goes through with its present wording, there could be a threat to privacy. The headline of the editorial is "A Threat to Mail Privacy", and it reads in part:
The new act would make the prosecution of those who illegally open private letters more difficult, and it would lessen the penalties that may apply to those found guilty of the offence.
Members of Parliament should be aware of this provision, study it closely, and ensure that the sanctity of the mail remains intact and that the privacy of Canadians is not threatened by the proposals in this legislation.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate to the minister that we are glad that he is coming before the standing joint committee. However, we hope that it is not a matter of courtesy to the committee, but a matter that the government has accepted the principle that the committee was correct when it asked that the regulation-making authority contained in the bill be sent to it for expert scrutiny and that this committee should have the right to make amendments to the regulations if necessary.
I would point out to the minister the concerns which I have about the relationship between this legislation, the Crown corporation bill which we tabled last year, and the bill which may come down later this session. I would also express on behalf of hon. members of my side concern about the question of the privacy of mail in Canada. That privacy must remain inviolable and the government should not be trying to sneak in through the back door reductions to the privacy of mail for Canadians under the guise of creating a Post Office Crown corporation.
If the government can meet these objections, I think it would be possible for Parliament to move on this legislation and to create a structure for Crown corporations which will allow employees of the Post Office to continue with the pride which has existed historically in the Post Office and which will allow Canadians the assurance that the mail will go through efficiently and on time.
