BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-212, to amend the British North America Act, 1867, (native status, treaties and aboriginal rights) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to entrench in the Canadian Constitution those rights belonging to our aboriginal peoples, the Indian, status and non-status; the Inuit and the Metis. Among those rights are their rights to land, their aboriginal rights, their rights to resources, their rights to govern themselves as they see fit, their treaty rights, and so on. I will describe these in greater detail later.
The purpose for wanting to entrench these rights is that they have been continually eroded over the last 100 years by the legislative assemblies of the provinces and by the federal government. By entrenching these rights in the constitution, we would hope to put them beyond the ordinary legislative processes of the federal and provincial governments so that they could not be touched in any other way except by constitutional amendment. I say that their rights have been abrogated, rescinded and reduced over the years. This is true with respect to Indian reserve lands, their fishing rights, their hunting rights, and with respect to their rights to govern themselves as they did before the Europeans came.
The ideas in this bill are not completely my own. These are ideas I have heard over the years from attending Indian conferences and Inuit conferences. They are ideas formulated by examining resolutions adopted at those conferences and by sitting and listening to aboriginal peoples all over Canada. What I have tried to do is put in a form of a bill what I perceive their wishes to be, and with which I agreed.
I must say that 1 drafted this bill last spring. When 1 drafted it and presented it to the House of Commons for inclusion in the list of bills, I realized it was not the best possible bill, that it was subject to some defects and could be much better. Over the months which passed since last spring, better ideas on the subject have been presented. In the speech the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) made on the constitution a few weeks ago, he presented some ideas with respect to these matters which are an improvement on my own. He brought these forward from the ITC and other inuit organizations.
As well, the National Indian Brotherhood has been working on this matter in recent months. They recently came up with what I believe to be a much better draft for these rights than my bill. That having been said, the principles in my bill are fairly close to the principles in both the Inuit and NIB

November 20, 1980
Native Rights
proposals which have been distributed to members of Parliament in recent weeks.
In discussing the constitutional proposals presently before Parliament and now being discussed in committee in Room 200 of these Parliament Buildings, the government said they want to protect native rights in Canada. Consequently, they have put in the proposed resolution for a joint address to Her Majesty regarding the Constitution of Canada, article 24, which they say will protect and guarantee those rights for the time being.
I completely disagree with that suggestion. I want to explain that in this House. I attempted to do it in the very short period of time given to me the other day in committee when I discussed this matter with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). I hope I made a few points with him, but one is limited to five or seven minutes in that committee. I did not have much time to develop an argument. Article 24 presently reads:
The guarantee in this charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be construed as denying the existence of any other rights or freedoms that exist in Canada, including any rights or freedoms that pertain to the native peoples of Canada.
Any person who can read and reads this section slowly will conclude that little is protected when it says "the guarantee in this charter shall not be construed as denying the existence of any other rights or freedoms that pertain to the native peoples of Canada." In other words, it is only what is in this charter which will not deny any rights to native people. The article does not say that the rights of native people cannot be revised, abrogated or rescinded by other laws of federal or provincial governments, which is the real basis of my disagreement.
Even if you pass article 24 as it is, the Parliament of Canada could introduce a bill next week expropriating Indian land. The legislative assembly of a province could introduce a bill taking away hunting and fishing rights belonging to Indians. This could go on all over the country. All this article says is that there is nothing in the charter that will reduce Indian or native rights. It does not say that native rights cannot be reduced by any other bill or legislative measure. It is extremely defective in protecting native rights. That is not much better than nothing at all.
What could be done, and I hope the government will consider this seriously, is to amend the constitutional proposals to adopt some of the suggestions in my bill. Better still, it could use the proposals published by the National Indian Brotherhood which will be discussed before the standing committee, hopefully within a couple a weeks. Either they should completely revise article 24 with a series of other articles which will really protect Indian and native rights, or take some measures to make article 24 effective. That could be done very easily.
Some people ask why must these rights be entrenched in the constitution. I will deal with the different ones and go through them, starting with the easiest ones first. First, there is the matter of treaty rights. The Crown on behalf of Canada and the British Crown concluded treaties with many of the Indian groups in Canada when they came in the eighteenth and
nineteenth centuries because they were taking lands which belonged to these people, as well as their resources. They were overrunning territories these people had occupied for thousands of years when they were sovereign nations. They formed treaties with these people saying that in exchange for certain recognition, they would guarantee their rights.
Over the years the legislative bodies of this country, the Parliament of Canada and the legislative assemblies of the provinces, passed laws which took away those rights which were granted to the Indians in these treaties. I say it is wrong, and over the years the Indian people have said it is wrong. The government of the United States recognizes the treaties which they signed with native people prevail over ordinary legislation. They look on these treaties as international treaties. They have a special status. What the Indian people are asking, and what I am asking in my bill, is that treaty rights be entrenched in the constitution so they cannot be rescinded by ordinary legislation of the provinces or federal government. That is number one.
Second are the rights which were set out for the native people in this country, and that applies to the Indians, the Inuit and the Metis, in the royal proclamation of 1763. In that royal proclamation there are several sections guaranteeing the rights of Her Majesty's Indian, Inuit and so on. That document, which is supposed to be a constitutional document and in a sense should be entrenched, was never entrenched.
The legislative assemblies of the provinces and the Parliament of Canada have taken away some of those rights. They have not respected the rights set out in the royal proclamation of 1763. The courts have not respected them. They looked on that royal proclamation as something less than an entrenched constitutional document. The second thing I ask in my bill and the native people ask in their document is that all the rights in the royal proclamation of 1763 be entrenched in the constitution so they will be protected from the ordinary legislative processes.
The third, aboriginal rights, is more difficult. Some members of Parliament ask what they are. They say because we do not know what they are, we cannot entrench them. In a nutshell, aboriginal rights are all those rights which the Indian nations and Inuit nations possessed in this country before the coming of the Europeans. I must say that I am incensed every time I hear my colleagues talk about the two founding peoples of this country as being the English and the French. They speak as though they were the first to come here, as though no civilization existed here before that. They say that as though the people who were here before were not people at all. However, they were people. They had civilization, societies, laws, languages, cultures and economies. Consequently they had rights, and these are their aboriginal rights.
When the Europeans came here, the French, English and Spanish, in most cases they did not get contracts with the aboriginal peoples. They did not make contracts by which these people gave up their rights legally in accordance with the European legal system. In most cases they took them by force of numbers, arms and, in some cases, advanced technology. They just overran these people.
November 20, 1980

Consequently, in accordance with our own principles of justice, if you have a right and you have never given it up, you still have it. That is what we mean by aboriginal rights. These people had rights then. They have never given them up. They never agreed to the BN A Act of 1867. They were not even asked for their agreement. They never gave up many of their lands. Some of them gave up some of their lands in treaties, but treaties only cover a small part of this country where native people have lived. Aboriginal rights existed, and they still exist.
A few years ago the Government of Canada agreed to negotiate the exact terms of those aboriginal rights with the original people of this country-the Indians, the Inuit and the Metis-and it is in the process of negotiating those rights. In its policies the government agreed that they exist, but now it is just a question of defining them in particular, and I am saying that that policy the government has adopted that there are aboriginal rights, even though we do not know what they are in detail, should be put in the constitution so that those aboriginal rights will not continually be eroded by the Parliament of Canada and by the legislatures of the provinces.
That is taking place, even while the negotiations are going on. Lands which are claimed by different bands across the country and lands which are being claimed by Inuit communities are being sold to non-native peoples. Mineral rights are being granted in perpetuity to large multinational corporations. By the time agreements are reached, we will be in a situation in which it will be very difficult to return those lands to the peoples who really have rights to them.
When we have put questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) with respect to the negotiation of these matters and their entrenchment in the present constitutional document which is before Parliament, they have answered time and again that they are interested in the subject but that they will do it after patriation and that it will be a matter of high priority once the constitution is brought to the country. I have said before, and I will say again, that that is not acceptable, because once the constitution is patriated we will have to go through that very difficult amending formula which is in the constitutional proposal.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
If the government has seen fit to proceed unilaterally on the rights of Anglophone minorities, Francophone minorities, mobility rights, the rights of women and the rights of the aged, which I approve, surely it should protect the rights of the original people of this country who number no more than perhaps 1,050,000 people. The government should certainly entrench those rights as well. It could easily be done. Different formula are already available. My bill is available. The NIB proposals are available. The Inuit Tapirisat proposals are available. It could be done even within the short deadline set by the government.
Native Rights
I maintain that justice demands that we do this in this country. Until this matter is settled it will continue to be a black mark against the majority peoples of this country, and if we think that the protests up to date have been sometimes stormy, as they were in about 1975 when Indians from all over the country marched on Parliament Hill and camped on Parliament Hill, they are going to be stormier still. The native people of this country will not rest until these things are entrenched. Sure they are going to Britain and to the United Nations, and they will go to other international bodies because they are not being listened to in this country.
It is a sad thing that they have to go abroad to get public attention with regard to their rights. In principle we do not like that, but when you have been denied so many times, you will use whatever means at your disposal, and that is what they are doing. I say that justice demands that we correct this. I see two eminent parliamentary secretaries here, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chenier), and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Irwin). I hope they will not give me the same answer they gave me on the adjournment debate a few weeks ago. I hope they will be able to tell this House that the government recognizes that article 24 of the constitutional proposal is really not adequate and that the government intends to amend that section to protect treaty rights, the rights in the Royal Proclamation of 1763, and aboriginal rights, and that they will be protected in a positive way in the proposal. As I said, they can borrow from my bill or from any other documents. I hope they will say that this will be done now and not after patriation.
Furthermore, I would be extremely pleased if they would do with my bill as has been done with other bills from time to time, that is, agree to refer the subject matter to the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution so that the joint committee can consider the proposals in my bill. In that way they will not be talked out or killed tonight as private members' proposals usually are.
I conclude by saying that 1 personally am committed to this cause. I think it is just. For me, not to do it is one of the most glaring injustices in this country, and I will continue to do everything in my power to work for the entrenchment of those rights. I ask the representatives of the government who are here this evening to agree to protect those rights in the way they should be protected.

subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this bill gives me to speak on the subject of the constitution, and I am particularly pleased to speak about this specific area which greatly concerns me.
I must congratulate the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) on the timing of his bill, which appears before the House at a time when the very treaties and special rights of our aboriginal people are threatened. I do not think I have ever heard this subject spoken about more succinctly and strongly. What the hon. member just said to us is right to the point. I agree with him 100 per cent.
4912

November 20, 1980
Native Rights
Obviously, the hon. member must have strongly suspected, or even knew, that the issue of native rights would be left out of the constitutional resolution, and it grieves me that a previous minister and former minister of Indian affairs was not listened to by his caucus and by the Liberal government.
Native people are threatened today by a government which is determined to alter the structure of Canada according to an artificial timetable. The bill which my colleague has presented to the House goes a long way toward reducing that threat.
The importance of this bill cannot be overestimated. It is of vital importance to the native people of our land, and it is of vital importance to all Canadians who wish to see simple justice prevail. If we believe in justice, for heaven's sake we must believe in what this bill is trying to tell the people of Canada.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has said that he would study and consider any written proposals on the constitution presented to him. This bill gives the minister an opportunity not only to study and consider this written proposal, but he can also demonstrate his good faith by supporting this bill. In addition to that, the minister would be recognizing the basic justice contained in this bill. The minister must recognize the basic justice in Bill C-212 because his party acknowledged the legitimacy of the native argument in a recently leaked document. This document is just another in a long line from the government. This time it is from the federal-provincial relations office, and it is entitled "Briefing material on Canada's native peoples and the constitution". What the document does is lay out the game plan of the government vis-a-vis how to handle the problem which will arise with respect to native people. It appears to have been written in the last two or three weeks.
I would like to quote from this brief which has emanated from this increasingly leaky ship of state. On page one it states, and I quote:
Native leaders would like to achieve goals in the patriation process which are remarkably similar to those of the federal government vis-a-vis the Canadian people as a whole.
If native goals are remarkably similar to the goals of the federal government on the constitutional resolution, one would assume that the federal government's sense of urgency with respect to native aspirations would be remarkably similar to that which it is expressing concerning the Canadian people as a whole. If the government denies the urgency or the legitimacy of the goals of the native people, then obviously it must be denying the legitimacy of its own goals concerning the constitution. The government can recognize both the legitimacy and urgency of the aboriginal goals by urging its supporters to vote in favour of Bill C-212. The two issues are not separate, but are remarkably similar.
Bill C-212 recognizes this relationship, and is designed to attack the injustice of trying to treat the native issue separately. The treaties and rights of the aboriginal people of Canada are a type of constitution for our first citizens. When the
patriation and amendment of our constitution is considered, we cannot separate this process from the constitution of the native people. Change in one automatically causes change in the other. Bill C-212 merely acts as the change in the native constitution to compensate for the change in the Canadian constitution.
The sad thing is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recognizes this relationship, but refuses to acknowledge it. This can be seen most vividly by a comparison of two documents written a matter of days apart. The first document is the one to which I have been referring-the briefing material on Canada's native peoples and the constitution. The second is a letter sent to the native leaders by the Prime Minister, dated October 30, 1980.
In the five-page letter to the native leaders, the Prime Minister said, and I quote:
In short, I believe that constitutional change after patriation will become easier, rather than harder-
In the brief, on the other hand, we are informed that:
-entrenching their rights will be enormously difficult after patriation, especially since a majority of the provinces would have to agree to changes which might benefit native peoples at the expense of provincial power.
Obviously, there is some difference between these two statements. The difference seems to be between public government policy and actual government policy. As usual, the native people are being subjected to double talk, half truths, and false promises.
The Prime Minister has told the leaders of the aboriginal people that they have nothing to worry about; that entrenchment will be easier after patriation. However, when he told the leadership this, he knew that, in truth, entrenchment would be more difficult after patriation. How can the aboriginal people be expected to trust the government to protect their rights after patriation of the constitution, when he misleads them on that very issue before patriation?
There is another area of conflict between these two documents, the public voice of the government and the private voice of the government. The private voice of the government says:
The status of Indian treaties and of existing and future native land claims is not clarified by the proposals of section 24.
The public voice of the government, The Prime Minister, says:
Let me respond to your worries by saying that 1 am personally convinced that your people will lose nothing in this act of patriation.
1 say, balderdash! The native people will lose something for certain; they will lose the opportunity to entrench their rights and treaties. Clause 24 works against the entrenchment of rights and treaties. By failing to entrench clause 24, the government leaves the question of native rights at the mercy of the provinces, which it acknowledges, will not likely agree on this issue. Bill C-212 removes any doubt on this matter. Bill C-212 would guarantee the rights and treaties of the aboriginal peoples. The government has before it today an opportunity to rectify this glaring deficiency.
Bill C-212 has another characteristic which should appeal to the government. It would be quick. Speed appears to be an
November 20, 1980

overriding consideration in this brief on native people and the constitution. Let me quote once more from this informative document. It reads:
Given the need to act, therefore, and the government's timetable, entrenchment of native rights before patriation is not possible.
Later, on that same page, the brief goes on to say:
The native leaders argue that the possibility of federal unilateral action on the constitution under present conditions includes an opportunity for the federal government to unilaterally entrench native rights. This opportunity would be lost after patriation. The answer here again is that the government has decided to move quickly.
The government does not deny the truth in the native leaders' argument. It argues that the artificial timetable imposed on Parliament is the only real time constraint. If the government is determined to ram through patriation within such an unrealistic time-frame, the very least it could do would be to ensure that the rights and treaties of the aboriginal people are protected. Bill C-212 performs this function.
The government has stated that it does not feel the native people have anything to fear from the patriation of the constitution-that it will act to protect those aboriginal rights and treaties to the maximum. A fine illustration of this commitment was recently given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Simmons). Last month the acid-tongued member for Burin-St. George's stated in a speech to the Canadian Institute of Forestry in Ottawa:
The federal government itself owns or controls about 18 per cent of Canada's forest land. While it is true that most of this land is in the north, there are over one million hectares of forest land in Indian reservations within provincial boundaries.
This unilateral patriation of Indian land should come as a surprise to all the native people of Canada. Until the speech was made, they were under the impression that forest land on their reservations was in fact their own property. I am sure the parliamentary secretary was looking to the future when the constitution has been patriated and he can more easily accomplish this land grab. I would be very pleased if we could surprise the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment today by robbing him of that opportunity. We could do this by simply passing Bill C-212. The bill before us would protect the aboriginal people from this sort of highhanded approach to their treaties, rights and heritage.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) for giving me this opportunity to support his bill. It is an expression of his real concern for the aboriginal people of Canada that this vital piece of legislation is before us today. 1 can only hope that his colleagues will take up the challenge which he has presented to them and vote in favour of this amendment to the British North America Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to applaud the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) and to congratulate the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) for putting forward a bill which recognizes the aboriginal people of Canada. I am delighted and charmed that members of the other two parties would feel
Native Rights
so strongly about concerns for which my people and the Indians have been fighting for many years.
This bill contains two parts, one on Indians and one on Inuit. It is with reference to the Inuit that 1 should like to speak, albeit briefly. The underlying point is, I think, to advocate official recognition of the aboriginal rights of Inuit in the Canadian constitution as well as establishing mechanisms for acquiring some economic and political control over the structures which rule us in the north.
The government would have us believe that Clause 24, of the charter of rights-in my view, the latest insult to the natives of Canada-is adequate as it protects existing rights and freedoms. These so-called existing rights are contained in the Indian Act which is nothing but an administrative statute which can be overridden by Parliament at any time.
The BNA Act when drafted did not even mention Inuit. It merely gave the federal government power over "Indians and land reserved for Indians." Although the 1924 amendment to the Indian Act placed Eskimos under the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, it did not mention property or any application of the Indian Act to Eskimos. In fact, former prime minister Arthur Meighen said:
The best policy we can adopt toward Eskimos is to leave them alone.
Such is not the case today. Their lands and their rights are being encroached upon in many ways which are detrimental to their livelihood. The section on Eskimo affairs was repealed in 1930. As far as Inuit are concerned, the Indian Act still does not apply to us; and we certainly do not mean any reflection upon the Indian people of this country. So much for protecting Inuit rights.
In the past the protection of our rights as Inuit was not as pressing as it is today. The past three decades have seen many changes take place in the north. Government activities prior to 1950 were minimal. Economic livelihood was largely land and sea based, and the fur trade provided the main source of contact between Inuit and southern society. Increased government presence in the north created a situation whereby Inuit were compelled to learn about southern-styled or world-styled politics, largely out of necessity rather than genuine or spontaneous interest. I am here in Ottawa out of spontaneous interest rather than genuine interest, and I say this in all truth. I do not have any heart to be here, but I must be here because of the encroachment on my people about which I spoke.
This holds true today. The Government of Canada has proposed the patriation of the Constitution of Canada. The constitutional resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not recognize the collective aboriginal rights of Inuit. This may not have been important to us 30 years ago, but the implications today are somewhat frightening.
Especially after the sell-out to the United States every year, the north is now viewed as Canada's and North America's resource warehouse to be developed as needed. The 1980 national energy program indicated that the need for Arctic gas in Canadian markets may not arise for many years, yet we
*

November 20, 1980
Native Rights
should press ahead with exploration so that Canadians may have a secure source of oil and gas available as a safety net for the future. In the face of large-scale resource development, the traditional economy and lifestyles of Inuit, not to mention rights, are subject to constant strain.
We are talking here about very major social and economic changes. Some have occurred already, but more are on the horizon. The constitutional guarantees which Inuit seek will be proposed to the Joint House of Commons and Senate Committee on the Constitution when the Inuit committee on national issues appear before it. Constitutional recognition of the aboriginal rights and freedoms of Inuit will not solve all our present or future problems, but it will provide us with a base from which we can work toward solutions.
I am sure this was the intention of Bill C-212 and I heartily support it. While I agree with the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that the wording of the bill is not as exact as we would like it, we heartily support the principle and spirit of it.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) clearly set out the government's position in this regard in his letter of October 30, 1980, to the three presidents of the major native organizations. He made the following points: he is personally committed to ensuring that the voices of native peoples are heard in the process of framing a new constitution and that the government remains committed to working with them toward

Mr. Speaker, I could not be more honest because it is the truth. The steps being taken will not reduce the current status of native peoples in Canada. Section 91(4) of the BNA Act, which gives responsibility over Indians to the federal government, will be unchanged. The status of treaties will be unchanged. The Indian Act continues to be in force. The resource transfer agreements embodied in the British North America Act will continue to limit the application of provincial game laws in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba with respect to the right of Indians to hunt, trap and fish for food. In addition, the government remains committed to the process of dealing with the claims of native groups.
Section 24 of the constitution continues the existing protection of the native people's way of life by assuring that any rights or freedoms that pertain to the native peoples of Canada shall not be abrogated by the introduction of a guarantee in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of certain rights and freedoms for all Canadians. This section is purposefully open-ended. There is, as I have said before, the possibility of future entrenchment of additional rights in the constitution such as those demanded by native peoples.

In short, 1 can only congratulate my colleague the hon. Warren Allmand for his interest in the rights and interests of the native peoples, Bill C-212 being an obvious proof of that. However, while I agree on the objectives, I must indicate that I do not share his view on the means to protect their rights and to entrench them in the constitution. The government's position, as stated in the resolution on the constitution and in the various speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dealing with the participation of the native peoples in the constitutional review process, is based on consultation and co-operation with them and, when necessary, with the provinces.

We believe that a matter as important as the identification and entrenchment of native rights must take this approach if it is to succeed in the long run.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to what the hon. member has just said I would profoundly disagree with virtually all of it. I do not think it is unparliamentary to say it represents nothing but hypocricy from the first word he said to the last. As the Civil Liberties Association pointed out in the committee hearings, what the so-called rights in this charter of rights represent is a diminution in the rights of Canadians. For instance, the first section says:
Native Rights
-subject only to such reasonable limits as are generally accepted in a free and democratic society with a parliamentary system of government.
As you will be aware, Mr. Speaker, the Civil Liberties Association and a number of other groups have indicated, these words give the government the right to use the War Measures Act and provide other ways in it they can encroach on the freedom of Canadians and say there is a constitutional right to use such measures. Looking through these so-called rights and freedoms I suggest we will hear from all of the thoughtful people appearing before the committee that they represent a reduction rather than an entrenchment of any rights for Canadians. The section with respect to native rights is, perhaps, as hypocritical as any other in the charter. I will read it:
The guarantee in this charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be construed as denying the existence of any other rights or freedoms that exist in Canada, including any rights or freedoms that pertain to the native peoples of Canada.
I suggest that "native peoples of Canada" is an afterthought. I ask the hon. member on the government side who just spoke: what single native person, native group or association has spoken in favour of section 24? I submit there is not a single native person in Canada who agrees with what 1 call the nonsense we have just heard from the parliamentary secretary. That ought to be a pretty good test of whether the native people in Canada have any conviction that the government is trying to protect their rights. One could give a litany of what members opposite have done over many years to try to reduce the rights of native people, rights under their treaties and under the Indian Act. Incidentally, I would agree with everything that has been said by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand). I think he expressed sentiments, as did the hon. member from the eastern Arctic, which the vast majority of members in my party agree with.
The point government members do not understand is that many natives in this country believe they have a special relationship with the monarch, that is, the monarch of Great Britain. This was better said by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace than I have said it. The native people feel that this relationship is severed by this charter of rights and that they would be losing something. This has been made clear to every member in this House. The special relationship they value has been referred to many times; they talk about the honour of the Queen and say it should not be jeopardized by violating their treaty rights and other of their accumulated rights.
The subject of aboriginal title has been mentioned as well. I do not think the parliamentary secretary appreciates that the concept of aboriginal title has been recognized in civilized countries, including the United States, where aboriginal title has been bought out or terminated at a cost in compensation of some $4 billion. Members opposite do not even recognize aboriginal title despite their charter on the subject. I think it is time that members like the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace spoke individually to members of the Liberal caucus about this.

which touch on the regulatory aspects contemplated for the new Crown corporation, we are willing to pass the bill tonight.

Having said that, it is important that members give consideration to the question of what we are dealing with tonight because in many ways the deficit of the Post Office developed during the reign of the present emperor who is now over in Saudi Arabia or some place. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is drawing my attention to the fact that there is a time difference between Canada and where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is now being entertained.
Bill C-42 has been a necessity because of the mess which has been made of our postal system by successive Liberal administrations. Slow mail delivery has become a common joke as most of us know. The postal service is used as a synonym for government inefficiency. In many ways I would suggest we see in the post office a small example, or a microcosm of how this government over the years under the present Prime Minister has mismanaged the economy in Canada generally. The inefficiency and inadequacy of the government is reflected first in the Post Office, the subject that we are considering tonight and, second, on a much larger scale, throughout our entire economic fibre.
We have before us tonight the subject of the Post Office and the question whether it should be turned into a Crown corporation. If so, what powers should the Crown corporation possess? It is very strange that we should have this matter before us at a time when the post office is running a deficit of $400 million to $500 million. The "blue book" forecast the deficit for 1980-1981 at $425 million. Yet a member to our left, from the NDP caucus-some say the far left, but these lefties all look
Canada Post Corporation Act
the same to me-has the audacity to stand up in this House and say, "cut off the debate, I have other matters I want to get to". Mr. Speaker, here is something which is draining the public purse to the tune of over $400 million and our socialist friends, in their eagerness to support this Liberal government, are saying, "let us not discuss it too long. Let us get on to other matters".

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Your anger does not become you.
What is the matter with that?

I hear another socialist asking, "What is the matter with that?" The saying used to be, "What's a million?" Now they are saying, "What's $400 million?" That, in part, is what I want to deal with tonight.
Let us not forget that when the emperor took power in this country total revenues and expenditures with respect to the post office were approximately $300 million. Now we find that expenditures have gone up to $1,762 million. Revenues, as I have just indicated, are far, far behind that figure.
The significant thing, and I want to put this on the record very early, is the extent to which this government has mismanaged the Post Office. In the fiscal year 1967 to 1968-I hope hon. members will make a note of these figures-the total mail volume by number of pieces was 4.9 billion. In the 1979-1980 fiscal year the total number of handled items in the Post Office was 6.4 billion. In short, there was a 30 per cent increase. Normally, with the tremendous degree of automation we have paid for in the Post Office one would expect there would be a saving on costs, meaning less revenue would be needed, and that the deficit, if anything, would contract, not expand. One would expect that the number of workers in the Post Office today would be fewer rather than more. If there has been a 30 per cent increase in the number of items handled, then presumably, with today's automation-the sorting machines and all of the advanced technology-fewer people would be needed to handle what the Post Office is doing.
Let me put some more figures on the record. As I have said, the number of pieces handled by the Post Office has gone up 30 per cent. The total number of people working for the Post Office, based on the estimates for the years 1967-1968 compared to the estimates for the year 1979-1980 has gone up 64 per cent. In short, in that period while the emperor has been in power, notwithstanding that activity in the Post Office has gone up only 30 per cent, the number of employees has risen by 64 per cent. That figure has risen from 36,875 workers in the fiscal year 1968 to the current 60,317 workers in 1979-1980.
In spite of what our socialist friends may want to say, surely the nation would want us to ask why has the number of employees in the Post Office increased at a rate more than double the rise in the actual number of items being handled by the Post Office?
That is only part of the story, Mr. Speaker. If you like, maybe I can put that into more meaningful language and point out that in 1968 every worker in the Post Office from the top down handled 132,000 items. Today each worker handles

November 20, 1980
Canada Post Corporation Act
106,000 items. What has gone wrong? With the massive amount of money we have spent building new terminals, new facilities and new mail-handling equipment? Why are fewer items being handled per worker today compared to about ten years ago? Surely the emperor has to accept some responsibility for what has happened in this Crown corporation under his jurisdiction.
Again, that is only part of the story. As 1 have indicated, the amount of mail volume went up 30 per cent in those years 1 have referred to. I am pleased you are seated, Mr. Speaker, because when 1 give you the next group of figures, I know you will find it hard to stand. During that period, costs in the Post Office have gone up at a rate tenfold compared to the mail volume increase. Costs have gone up from $404 million to $1,762 million, or 336 per cent with the result the deficit we are left with has also gone up 316 per cent from $67 million to $279 million.
Surely with such a shameful record, bearing in mind that letter rates in the same period have climbed from five cents in 1968 to 17 cents at the present time, we should be able to turn to the government and ask what it plans to do now. In the coming years how does the government plan to correct this huge deficit it has allowed to run up?
As we know, in the budget which was delivered in this House on October 28, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) stated:
-I have, therefore, assumed that postal revenues will rise until they equal postal expenditures.
He said this after he mentioned that the new Crown corporation will be expected to cover its costs, the new Crown corporation being the Post Office Crown corporation which we are now considering. Here is the most serious thing to reveal to the Canadian public. How does he intend to make the post office break even? The fact is he intends to disguise the true picture in the post office by simply increasing revenues in the post office to offset the rising expenditures. He is proposing, through postal rate increases that will not pass through future budgets, to net out the high cost of running the Post Office against those revenues in order to take the deficit off the books. It will still be the Canadian public which has to pay the shot for this government's inadequacies.
They can fudge the books, but they cannot fudge the fact that Canadian postal rates will go up substantially if this government has its way. As opposed to running the Post Office efficiently, effectively and adequately, they are proposing to pass those added costs on to the Canadian public through postal rate increases. In short, it is not beyond the realm of possibility that postal rates, which have climbed from five cents in 1968 to 17 cents at the present time, will double before this government is through its mandate.
This brings me back to the question of what has happened. 1 know it is hoped-and we on this side believe there is a good chance this will happen-that by giving Crown corporation status to the Post Office, somehow there will be less friction in
future as opposed to past years with respect to labour negotiations in the Post Office. Here again it is wise to remind the members of this House that this friction in the post office is not traditional. For example, in the first 100 years there were only three strikes in the entire history of the Post Office in Canada. There was one in 1918, one in 1924 and one in 1965-that was a one-week strike in July over wages and it was by inside workers and letter carriers. Those were all the labour disruptions we had in our Post Office up until the time the emperor took power in this country.
The sheik.

The emperor or the sheik, whichever is senior. Here is the record of strikes since 1968. In July and August there was a three-week postal strike over wages. In February-March, 1970, there was a dispute in Montreal involving truck drivers represented by the CNTU over contracting of mail transport and job security. In May to September of that year there was a series of rotating strikes over wages and job security.
In October-November, 1971, there were several wildcat strikes in southwestern Ontario and the maritimes over the use of casual labour. In January, 1973, there were wildcat strikes after breakdowns in negotiations over wages and job classification. In April, 1974, there were sporadic local labour disruptions by inside postal workers culminating in a three-day nationwide strike. In February-March, 1975, there were five weeks of nationwide rotating strikes by maintenance workers. Truck drivers refused to cross picket lines. The dispute was characterized by lay-offs, walkouts and so-called "sick-outs".
From October to December of that year there was a seven-week strike by CUPW over contract demands. In October, 1976, there were four days of rotating strikes by CUPW over technological change. In September, 1978, there was a three-day strike by letter carriers over contract demands. In October, 1978, there was a strike by inside workers. Workers were ordered back to work by Parliament on that occasion.
The most recent position with respect to the postal workers is known to all of us. The fact that there were disruptions during the clerk's strike is well known. In short, I am trying to put on record that while in the first 101 years after confederation there was relative tranquility within the Post Office, under this government there has been a steady disruptive force at work as far as negotiations between the Post Office and the unions are concerned.
We must bear in mind what actually transpired during the period. In 1980 the average clerk working for the government earned $12,800 compared to an average postal salary of about $18,000. If we add the overtime the postal workers pick up on average, their salary is closer to $20,000. Currently, and certainly before the last settlement with the clerks, the clerks were getting about $12,800 compared to $18,000, possibly $20,000, for the postal workers.
In 1970, the average clerk earned $5,964 compared to a maximum Post Office salary of $6,450. In 1965 the clerk earned an average $4,600 a year compared to a 1966 max-
November 20, 1980

imum Post Office salary of $4,905. Therefore, there is no question that the gap has been widening. To put this widening gap in further perspective, 1965 was the year of the first postal strike since the twenties, while collective bargaining was introduced into the public service in 1967.
I put this on record because it might be suggested by some when I read the list of strikes and disturbances that perhaps, somehow, government has been keeping a tight fist and running things in a very cautious, severe manner. I suggest that when you review those figures, comparing them as 1 have with clerical salaries, it becomes clear that the postal workers have not done badly. There is now a substantial gap between their wage level and that of the clerks.
This is particularly important when you bear in mind what happened with the most recent settlement with the CUPW union. The present Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) virtually set aside the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), and awarded one of the most lavish, rich settlements we have seen in government settlements, if not in history, certainly in recent times. This in turn triggers more aggressive demands from others, not only in government circles, but in the private sector. We then find the government turning around and saying, as the Department of Finance said only last week, that unless workers are willing to begin accepting less in real wages, they are not going to get a handle on inflation.
Let me make two points about that. First, surely it is the government which has to be the pacesetter as far as the wage settlement pattern is concerned. Second, the government has to accept the responsibility for inflation in this country. Through its big spending, big deficits, printing of excess money and extensive borrowing the government is ensuring that inflation continues at the levels we are now experiencing. In short, the government puts us into a "Catch-22" position, in effect it triggers the inflation we experience and then blames others and asks them to accept sacrifice in order to get control of the very inflation it caused.
I know most of us have very little time to speak about this bill, but let me touch on a few other questions. Clause 17 of this bill is the clause which, hon. members will recall, deals with the tremendous regulatory powers of the Post Office. Granted, the present act gives it similar powers, but I think we must bear in mind that what we are now considering is the establishment of a Crown corporation which to some extent will be an entity unto itself. It will certainly be removed from this Parliament and, in turn, if we give the Post Office the same powers to make regulations and to make decisions as are now contained in the Post Office legislation and as are set out in clause 17 of the bill before us, I think we do this country a great disservice. I say this because when we start weighing the implications of where these regulations can lead the Post Office it becomes evident that it is a very dangerous monster we are letting loose if we do not put more restrictions in its way than are presently contemplated.
Canada Post Corporation Act
There is the whole question of competition. I know most of us have heard of various courier services which are indicating that they may be impeded in their activities if the Post Office is allowed to get almost unfettered control over who can carry various objects such as small parcels and so on, but most of us are perhaps not aware of how actively the Post Office has been trying to kill competition in those fields.
Let me simply refer to two examples. One is the United Parcel Service Canada Limited case, and the other is the Federal Express Corporation case. The first case involved an application to the Ontario Highway Transport Board for an extra-provincial operating licence and expanded service rights by United Parcel Service Canada Limited, commonly known as UPS.

speechtext: We would just like you to tell us that United Parcel is not Canadian.

The fact is that those who take the time-and I invite my colleagues to my left to check this-will find that after that tribunal reviewed the facts, it said "no" to the Postmaster General. The board made interesting observations. For example, it said:
The Post Office tendered evidence that in essence addressed the many-faceted national responsibilities with which it is seized. That the Post Office has played and continues to play a significant role in the national 'smalls'-
Apparently that is jargon in the trade meaning, I take it, small packages.
-transportation field is not in question here, and it is evident from the evidence tendered on its behalf that, for many, the service offered is satisfactory. It is also apparent from the growth of the alternative services in the 'smalls' field that the demands of the marketplace have changed and the Post Office service is not satisfactory to a growing section of the marketplace.
I emphasize that this was an independent tribunal which was asked to consider an application for a courier-type service. This tribunal heard out the Post Office and said "no" to its objection with respect to the granting of that licence. The board went on to say:
However, notwithstanding the growth of the latter market, the evidence indicates an over-all increase in the number of pieces being handled by Canada Post, attesting to the use of the mail by a large section of the public. The challenge to the Post Office with respect to retaining their share of this market relates not only to delivery times but to a pick-up service, improved proof of delivery, insurance, and claims settlement. Reference is also made to an earlier statement with respect to a pick-up service being generally available. The evidence presented fails to establish that this service had been made available with anything close to the alacrity promised. Granted, changes on the positive side, as

noted, the board is of the opinion that given the continued growth evidenced by the Post Office figures, the Post Office should be able to retain a significant share of the market without detriment to the varied services supplied to the public.
My time is running out, but I could go on and give hon. members the verdict with respect to the Federal Express Corporation case. This, interestingly enough, was a case considered on August 18, 1977, by the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission.
The committee rendered its judgment granting an application by Federal Express Corporation to operate a commercial air service to transport goods between Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and certain designated American cities. In short, the committee's judgment, which was subsequently asked to be appealed by the minister, was again that the Post Office should not be granted its objection. The Post Office should, in effect, be asked to compete with this type of service as opposed to relying on regulation to snuff out competition. I think this is one of the reasons we have to be very careful about the wording of Bill C-42. If we allow the Crown corporation to go ahead and get powers to regulate to the extent of actually snuffing out competition where it sees fit, it will be the Canadian consumer who will pay the penalty and be the big loser.
In light of the general information available about Crown corporations and in light of the Post Office's own record of performance-and I have referred only to two cases-it is disturbing to note that Bill C-42 could give the Post Office a virtual monopoly over the delivery of mail and parcel service.
As indicated earlier, we are generally concerned about the regulatory powers we would be giving to the Post Office in this bill. Besides limiting our freedoms, the Post Office could also pose a serious threat to our right to privacy. Clause 17(f) would give the Post Office the authority to make regulations allowing the opening of mail in order to determine whether it is undeliverable. At the same time the Post Office would be given the authority to define what is undeliverable. Clause 17 (l)(a) is to that effect. The total effect of clause 17, if put into law, would be to give the Post Office carte blanche, for example, to open mail.
Let me elaborate a little further on this point. It is not being argued that there is no need for government intervention in the economy. Rather, it is being said that government intervention should be kept to a minimum. That is our point. The present government is becoming increasingly interventionist, and I suggest that this bill will not only give the government the power to be interventionist but also that a Crown corporation responding to the government will also have such interventionist powers.
Milton Friedman, one of the most eminent economists of today, has stated, and I quote:
Economic freedom is an essential requisite for political freedom. By enabling people to co-operate with one another without coercion or central direction, it reduces the area over which political power is exercised. In addition, by dispersing power, the free market provides an offset to whatever concentration of
political power may arise. The combination of economic and political power in the same hands is a sure recipe for tyranny-
I mention that because I believe that when we see a chance for such powers to be put not only into the hands of the government but also into the hands of a Crown corporation responding to that government, it is time that we in this House stood up and asked that a halt be put to such a proposal.
Let the position of the official opposition be clear. We believe that the Crown corporation proposal should proceed. We should like to see it put in place as quickly as possible. But we have requested most sincerely that those provisions in the act which touch on the regulatory side should be referred to the appropriate joint committee of this House and the other place to enable that committee to deal specifically with the regulations and bring its supervision and suggestions to bear on the bill before it is passed by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
If the government would accept the suggestion that the subject matter of clauses 2, 3 and 17 of Bill C-42, the measure now before us, be referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments and that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours of our proposal, we would pass this bill before the evening runs out.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate this evening. I have been connected with the labour movement for some time. I should like to refer to the post office which is located in my constituency. What has happend to the post office we knew at one time? Not long ago, approximately six or seven years ago, one could mail a letter in Calgary destined for Edmonton. If it was mailed early in the morning, it would be received in the afternoon of the same day. Today the Post Office cannot deliver. Perhaps it will take a week, two weeks or even a month. Yesterday I received a telephone call from one of my constituents who had received a parcel in Calgary. It was mailed in Ontario, and it took 1.5 years for it to be delivered. I cannot believe the service has deteriorated from bad to worse. It is not only a concern of the average citizen who sends mail to a friend or relative. The service has absolutely failed the business community because of a lack of leadership in government. I readily understand why. It is because the head of the government is a philosopher who does not give any practical leadership.
Not only has morale in the Post Office deteriorated; employees of the Department of Employment and Immigration, to give one example, are frustrated, disappointed and disenchanted. It is very difficult to believe the type of situation which exists in the government. As a member of Parliament who has been here for only a short while I am beginning to understand the type of democracy which exists here. It is more of a dictatorial system than a democratic one. I did not experience such a system when I was a member of the legislative assembly of Alberta, and it disappointed me when I became a federal member of Parliament.
I remember that at one point the problem in Calgary was blamed on the lack of a new facility. After the new facility was built, approximately one or two years later, it was indicated that the equipment was very sophisticated and it would take the employees some time to learn how to operate it. Since that point the situation has worsened. Approximately a year ago there were 32 to 34 semi-trucks loaded with mail. They were backed up because they could not handle the situation. I can understand this problem to some degree because the Calgary sorting station sorts mail for the entire province of Alberta and part of the province of British Columbia.

Management is indicating that it is faced with obstruction from the bureaucracy in the government, and it blames the unions for its problems. I have met with labour and union people, and they blame management. Also it should be said that there are labour problems within the Post Office unions. I hope it is possible to correct them.
I am not too sure that the establishment of a Crown corporation will be the answer. Hopefully it will improve the situation, and 1 am prepared to go in that direction. But we must remember that the record of Crown corporations is not very good. As a matter of fact, the efficiency of Crown corporations under the Liberal government is very, very bad. 1 think that is a matter of record.
1 should like to deal with the question of hiring people, an area in which I have had some experience. A few people have aproached me asking how to apply for jobs in the Post Office. 1 have outlined the procedure, they have made applications, and some of them never even came close. On one occasion I had opportunity to review the procedure to which a person is subjected in order to qualify for a job, and I was told by a top person in the Post Office that he questioned whether even he would qualify. Certainly the test that is given is not a practical one. One might think it was designed not to attract people who would be interested in the job or people who would have pride and respect in the job. Some to whom I spoke were concerned and interested, and I asked them why they would work for the Post Office, especially when I knew many employees who were ashamed to admit that they worked for the Post Office because of its record of lousy service. One person likened it to wanting to be a policeman or fireman; he wanted to work for the Post Office. That particular person had a good education, his attitude was good, but he did not even come close to passing the test he was given in order to qualify. There is something radically wrong.
I wish I could be fully convinced that the establishment of a Crown corporation was the answer, that it would eliminate some of the bureaucracy. But as some parts of the bureaucracy are eliminated, others are created. I know the situation is worsening and possibly the establishment of a Crown corporation is the answer. Perhaps it will result in management and labour trying to work together for the first time.
1 cannot blame the trade union movement or even the workers. I blame management. Management has done a lousy job in the Post Office. Certainly we cannot compliment it. I think some surgical operation is necessary in the management area to correct the problem, and I am not fully convinced that it is the establishment of a Crown corporation.
It seems to me the service presently provided is directed more toward the delivery of junk mail. If people feel they have important mail, they send it by courier or find some other means of delivery. The private sector has reached the conclusion that it must find other ways and means of sending mail. In fact, technology has been developed in the area of electronics and telecommunications for sending mail. This will eliminate to some degree the Post Office service. If the Crown
corporation comes into being, if we are really rubber-stamping it, I should like an assurance from the minister at this time that it will expand into some other mechanical area such as data processing or whatever. I would like some assurance from the minister that it will remain as it is today under the same act. It will probably sharpen up the management. I would like to have those assurances from the minister but I see he is not in his place. As a matter of fact, I only see one minister sitting in the House right now listening to the discussion of this very important issue. That is most disappointing and discouraging.
What is the forum by which this Parliament processes its orders and legislation? I wonder if the minister will at one time or another give us an assurance that a Crown corporation will offer some improvement over the service we receive at the present time. I wonder if he will give us his assurance that there will be some co-operation between labour and management, at least much better than it is today when we have seen it at its worst. I hope that before we vote on this issue the ministers' will respond to some of these questions. I see only that the philosophy will not change under this government.
It is clear that few of the ministers-and I don't want to criticize them unduly-have experience in the areas for which they are responsible. I could pick out the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), neither of whom have had too much experience in the fields in which they are asked to perform. I realize that they do not have to know a great deal as long as they can be properly informed by their officials. I know that there are more capable people in the caucus of the Liberal party, although somehow it appears there is a kind of clique. Speaking of that clique, I know that as far as the constitution is concerned the whole Liberal caucus does not support the method the government is using to rush the constitution through. More time has been given to the Bank Act and to other issues of relatively minor importance than to the constitution, which is being railroaded.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope the minister will answer some of my questions.

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to repeal the Post Office Act and to create the Canada Post Corporation.
The Post Office is probably the most visible government service we have. Every day on most of our streets some person representing the Government of Canada goes from door to door. So, to a large extent, the federal government's reputation with ordinary people is determined by the effectiveness of the Post Office. That effectiveness has not been demonstrated and to a large extent the people of Canada mistrust the federal government because of the inept management of the Post Office.
The story going around my riding, where the Gateway is located, is that it costs 17 cents for the stamp-10 cents for storage and 7 cents for delivery. It is the biggest storage warehouse in the country.
November 20, 1980

I would like to go through some of the clauses of the bill. One of the most disappointing is clause 5(2) which reads:
(2) While maintaining basic customary postal service, the corporation, in carrying out its objects, shall have regard to-
The clause continues in paragraph (d) "the need to maintain a corporate identity .. among other things. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Kushner) spoke of a parcel that took a year and a half to be delivered. I received a parcel myself in Mississauga South from the riding of the hon. member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren) sent by the Dictaphone Company in Etobicoke. It was mailed on January 17, 1971, and it arrived at my law office on August 29, 1980.
It would be unfair of me, with respect to a bill such as this, if I did not read into the record just two pieces of correspondence which I received as a member of Parliament. The first is from Mumby and Associates, a small business. It reads in part as follows:
Many of my business associates cannot understand why I do not use couriers, at least for my salesmen across Canada. The fact remains that I cannot afford this. Even if 1 considered using couriers, the most that this would accomplish would be to improve the orders written by my salesmen. It would not improve the orders sent directly by my customers. I am losing customers at an astounding rate, simply due to the existing postal service.
The other letter is from Gladys Hudspeth, a pensioner from England. She wrote:
My husband and I are awaiting his veterans cheque from England. It is two weeks overdue,-now this happened also in July, at which time we cabled Britain and also made a long distance call. Reply was, cheque mailed as usual, hold-up must be your end. Well, when we emigrated to Canada in 1954, we could be sure of airmail letters arriving either point, in the space of three or four days. However, computers and the postal code came along, to speed up delivery. Local mail also takes ten days-
Mr. Speaker, it is not just "the customary service" that we have been receiving. It is a disgrace that this bill should refer to "customary service" because the customary service we have been receiving is just awful-inexcusable. More important, sir, is clause (2)(c) which says:
(c) the desirability of utilizing the human resources of the corporation in a manner that will both attain the objects of the corporation and ensure the commitment and dedication of its employees to the attainment of those objects;
The Gateway Post Office is in my city. If the minister were here I would remind him of a question I asked when I was in this House is 1973. At that time I asked him about a special delivery letter from Regina to Mississauga. There is air service between those two cities and the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, we are building one of the most modern mail handling centres in the hon. member's constituency; as soon as this is done, I am sure the service will be excellent in that region.
This is the same minister who said that to me on December 6, 1973, in this House. Well, what has happened? How do we use the human resources?
Let me read into the record another letter, from James Dickson, 2395 Homelands Drive, in the City of Mississauga. He writes:
As you know, every year, the Post Office calls Manpower to send them some Christmas help. I responded and began work Nov. 22, 1979, at a rate of $4.10 per hour on a 7'/2-hour day. When I signed up, a paper I signed at that time
Canada Post Corporation Act
indicated that I would be receiving a pay cheque on Dec. 21, a little late but in time for Christmas. A week before this time, I was talking with Tom Mansfield, a clerk where I worked at the Annex at 1400 Lakeshore Road East, Mississauga, and he said that we probably wouldn't be getting our money in time as they had been mailed from Ottawa and couldn't be found.
Later, I called the pay department at Gateway and was told that I should not expect anything until mid-January.
I will not read the whole letter but let me go through the figures.
My cheque was for $429.21. This was for a pay period in which I had worked 165 hours which would gross at $676.50, a difference of $247.29. As no statement of deductions was included, this can only be for taxes. At this pay scale, they took $100 too much.
The man received his cheque in January. That is the kind of promise which is made to people working at the Post Office, the kind of performance taking place and the way in which many people are handled.
On Saturday, I had a long chat with a Barry Dann, 1015 Roosevelt Avenue in Mississauga. He has been with the Post Office for four years, but not as a permanent employee because there are ways of getting around union organization problems and that is to hire people on consecutive six-month terms. No wonder there are problems. This man has had eight consecutive six-month terms but because he opened his mouth and began to talk to people like members of Parliament, he will not have another six-month term.
Let us put on the record of this House what really happened. This man has been working as a cleaner. His job is to work under a machine which is called the bulk mail handling machine at Gateway. The bulk mail at Gateway is handled by a supervisor who is 26 years old, who has no university education or real academic training whatsoever. It is believed by the union people that he was put there merely because he knew someone. In any event, the major problem in this enterprise is that there is a machine which is supposed to handle bulk mail.
Earlier in this session I spoke of a machine called an elephant which is located at Gateway. Apparently this machine, which is used for sorting, destroys almost as many packages as it sorts on some days. This man's job is to sweep under the elephant. Most of the material from the elephant goes to a place called the UMO, the undeliverable mail office. In many cases the mail is so smashed up and so undeliverable that when people ask the Post Office what happened to their parcel rather than declare how badly it was smashed up by the machinery, they say that it must have been stolen and that they will pay for it.
I am told that there is nothing like the theft which is supposed to take place in the Post Office. In fact, a great deal of the material which is destroyed or lost is destroyed by the machinery and by the system, and that is part of the problem. There is in Mississauga an annex down at 1400 Blakeshore Road, as I have already mentioned. That little annex used to be Canadian Arsenals, but now it is used to sort bulk mail. There are 200 people at the Canadian Arsenal annex who sort

50 per cent of the mail, that is sorted by 2,000 employees at the bulk mail centre at Gateway.
Those are just some of the management situations and problems in the Post Office. When we hear about honest, working people going on strike, walking off the job or filing grievances, the truth of the matter is that these people are not rebels or rabble rousers. They are hard-working people who want to do a day's work for a day's pay, but who want to be treated as people. They do not want to be pushed around or put on ten consecutive day shifts. I cannot imagine working ten days straight and then having four days off. It could just as easily be a five-day shift with two days off but that is impossible for this organization.
This organization makes its own rules. They merely forget the contract and make their own rules to the point at which even junior management people are filing grievances. The situation is unbelievable. Surely if we are to have a Crown corporation bill we had better do something to improve the customary services, particularly in the area of human resources.
It has been suggested that making the Post Office a Crown corporation will simplify matters. At the present time the Department of Supply and Services must supply the materials for the Post Office, the Department of Public Works must look after the buildings and the Treasury Board looks after wages and terms of employment. It does not need to be that way. There is no reason in the world why the Post Office Act could not be changed to operate the Post Office as a department of government with the specific right to do its own contacting, pay its own people and buy its own supplies.
There is nothing magic about having to refer all the buildings to the Public Works, all the supplies to Supply and Services and all the pay scales to Treasury Board. There is no need for this diversity, but it has to be the condition and the excuse for turning the Post Office into a Crown corporation. Perhaps it is nothing but an excuse to get the Post Office out of the limelight of public opinion and away from the scrutiny of the House of Commons. Perhaps it is just an excuse to get the terrible situation which exists in the Post Office one step removed from the political process.
If there is no possibility of public scrutiny, people will be deprived of any easy method to make complaints through their members of Parliament. I am glad the minister is present now because I would like to go over the record since this government took office. Its first Postmaster General was the Hon. Eric Kierans who ran the deficit from $68 million to $100 million. The next Postmaster General, the Hon. Pierre Cote, was much better because he only had $77 million deficit. Then the minister here pushed it up to $177.2 million. The hon. Bryce Mackasey was really good because he banged it up to $546 million. However, he was not the expert. It is the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) who achieved the top record of $578.8 million.
You did not mention John Fraser.
I am about to mention the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). During his year it was only $279 million.
You mean six months.

I mean for the whole fiscal year from March, when he was not responsible, right through to March 31 this year.
The present Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) is projecting a deficit of over $400 million, and we will give him credit for March through to March. One begins to wonder why, all of a sudden, one minister is able to keep the deficit down to $279 million while ministers of the Liberal party get it into the real big figures.
Are you saying the Liberals screwed up the Post Office?

The hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) has said that the Liberals have screwed up the Post Office, and the Canadian public knows that. The real question is, "will this Crown corporation improve things?" Perhaps if there is no postmaster general things will improve.
This bill will go to committee and I am pleased the minister has agreed to refer clauses 2, 3 and 17 to the standing joint committee; we will certainly give him time before ten o'clock to make the necessary motions. I would like to explain to the minister the reason clause 2 must be referred to that committee. It is because it is the section which defines such terms as "mail" as being "mailable matter" from the time it is deposited at a post office to the time it is delivered. However, it goes on to say, "mail conveyance means any physical, electronic, optical or other means used to transmit mail". The definition of transmit is, "transmit" means to send from one place to another place by any physical, electronic, optical or other means."
When you define that the post office has the right to declare what a letter is by clause 17, and declare what constitutes mail, then you find that the post office, with this regulatory power, has the right to determine that every transmission, whether oral or written or transmitted, may well be a letter and therefore mailable matter and within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Post Office. That is why all those clauses should be referred. We are going to demand some good explanations for the regulatory powers which the bill appropriates to this corporation.
I always wonder why any organization should have a monopoly. One of the advantages of a system is to have competing services. In a sense, competition for the post office at the present time is the courier service. Indeed, as you know, Mr. Speaker, even ministers of the Crown have used courier service and I would not be surprised if the Postmaster General uses a courier. What about the telegraph and telephone system? It is unfair that we should have one organization with a monopoly. As long as we have competition, we have some-
