thing by which to judge a service. It is important, in my view, that clause 14 dealing with a monopoly situation should be very seriously curtailed. Surely private individuals should be able to set up a service. Unless the postal service is so disgraceful, any private organization cannot conceivably make a profit. But if they can make a profit, it demonstrates how disgraceful the service is. Competition would give us something by which we can judge services and something by which we can determine whether or not we have a proper post office.
Another of my hon. friend's wishes to speak tonight for a few moments, but I have one more clause I want to refer to the minister. It concerns the penal sections in clauses 40 to 53. I particularly want to refer the minister to clause 43. Under clause 43, if a person delivers a letter bomb, it is just an offence under the Post Office Act. It is not an offence under the Criminal Code. I submit that an offence under clause 43 should at least be made a Criminal Code offence so that anyone who commits it by mailing any explosive, dangerous or destructive substance, or anything likely to injure or damage property or persons should be guilty of an indictable offence under the Criminal Code, not just under the regulatory effects of the Post Office.
I wonder why under those criminal sections it is illegal for you or me to sell somebody postage stamps, Mr. Speaker. Surely we are entitled to sell one another postage stamps, but that is an offence under this act. It strikes me there are a number of similar provisions under the act where it is really difficult to determine why certain actions should be made offences and subject to penalty.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by considering the major thrust of Bill C-42, which would create a Crown corporation to be called the Canada Post Corporation.
In my other emanations, prior to my election to Parliament, I was for several years counsel to government. While I held that role, many people would come to me from the public service and suggest that their governmental activity, be it a department, a commission or a board, ought to be continued and carried on as a Crown corporation. Apparently there the myth had developed that government activities, if carried on by a Crown corporation, would automatically become effective, efficient and more mindful of the costs and expenses involved in the administration. That is a myth which might well be perpetuated in this bill. The postal service in Canada is not going to change for the better by merely enacting a piece of legislation which characterizes the postal services as a Crown corporation rather than a department of the Government of Canada. It is only the people who are concerned and involved in the provision of that service who can change its nature and develop a more efficient and effective postal service for Canada.
We do not want to be fooled by the myth of a Crown corporation. We must keep in mind the people who will be operating the postal service, whether they act through the medium of a Crown corporation, a commission or any other form of government organization. Let us think about those
Canada Post Corporation Act
people for a moment. There are 66,000 people, as I understand it, who are now involved in the postal service in Canada. This is a force not much smaller than the Canadian Armed Forces, which number approximately 75,000 to 80,000 people. So we have a vast number of people involved in this transfer. It is on their shoulders that we have to rest the responsibility for the improvement in the postal service which we hope will be brought about by the bill before us.
We have all heard in this debate about the problems which have arisen as a result of the poor labour relations which have existed in the Post Office. I am not one who would deny to any working Canadian the right to a living wage. Indeed, the postal workers for many years were in exactly that position. They did not receive, through their employment, a living wage.
I would like to think, and I believe it is the case, that that problem has to a great extent been overcome. Postal employees now receive what by Canadian standards ought to be and can be regarded as a living wage. That is not to say they ought not to be protected from inflation and other cost factors which affect their ability to provide a living for themselves and their families. But we must put labour relations within the post office-be it a Crown corporation or a government department-on a sound basis. In other words, it must be put on a basis which is sensible and in accord with Canadian traditions applicable to labour-management relations.
What does this new bill do to establish that kind of relationship between the employees of the Post Office and the management of the post office? I have to answer that question by saying it does nothing. It contains only minor technical, mechanical provisions providing for the transfer of employment rights and benefits. What it may give, and what we all hope it will give, is new life to the postal service. In other words, a chance to start again, to get on a new road which will lead to a more effective labour-management relationship and one which will avoid the strikes which have partly wrecked our economy in some areas in the past. So what we look for in a new bill is a new life for the post office.
Let me deal briefly with some other aspects of this transfer to a Crown corporation. I do not want anyone in Canada to be fooled by this device. We think of the business of government as being similar to the business of industry. But it is not, Mr. Speaker. The two are entirely different. The obligation of the Government of Canada is to provide the services which are required to enable this nation to reach its goals and carry on to benefit all Canadians. Under this bill we are asking the new corporation to take over an organization which in 1978-1979 had a deficit of a half a billion dollars. Its revenues of $1.1 billion were that much less than its expenses of $1.5 billion. You have to ask yourself, how can a new business start out with that kind of deficit. The answer comes back immediately. It must seek new revenues or increase its current revenues. There is only one way the Post Office can overcome the deficit with which it is now faced. That is to raise the rates of ordinary mail. By that I mean the letter rate.

November 20, 1980
Canada Post Corporation Act
My hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) is somewhat of an authority on this. He tells me that in the ten-year period between 1968 and 1979, the letter rate tripled from six cents to 17 cents. It is his belief it will increase dramatically over the next few months. When we look at these facts and figures, we find very quickly that we must agree with him. Canadians ought to be warned that they look forward to a letter rate very substantially higher than the present 17-cent ordinary letter rate. Canadians ought to be warned by this if they want a corporation whose goal and aim is to improve the postal service. If it is indeed the wish of Canadians and parliamentarians to put the postal service on a more sound financial basis, we have to pay the price. That price will be an increased letter rate.
Many people across this country who operate small businesses are very much dependent on the postal service. I often find myself in that position. During periods of postal strikes, cutbacks and delays in service, it is very difficult to operate a small business which depends on service to customers and utilization of the postal service. In that connection, we are very mindful of the monopoly that will be continued by the Canada Post Corporation under this new legislation. That monopoly prevents Canadians who have to depend upon the postal service from having any real alternative.
Notwithstanding this, there has grown up in most parts of Canada courier services and similar types of arrangements whereby mail material can be delivered through means other than the post office. Anyone who has operated a small business in this country during a period in which postal services have been withdrawn appreciates the existence of this courier service. I hope this new legislation and the monopoly which has been given to the postal service will not result in the persecution and prosecution of the courier services which have grown up around the country and which have been so effective in emergency situations when postal services were withdrawn.
I am sure all hon. members are aware that we need a proper balance between private sector courier services and the postal service of the Government of Canada. We cannot expect our public postal service to bear all the costs of postal service from which no profit can be received and allow private industry access to the profitable services. We always face the problem of balancing rates between government and the private sector. I hope the minister and those charged with the administration of this bill will keep this in mind.
I wish to speak briefly about what 1 consider the real pith and substance of the issue before us which is the service to the customers, to all who must use the postal service. During the course of this debate, other members have mentioned some of the horror stories relating to the postal service in the past. 1 could do so as well. However, I will cite just one instance in my constituency in the area known as the Kearney Lake Road. Within the space of a few hundred feet on one public highway, there are three levels of postal service. A few of the residents have access to regular city service. One hundred feet down the road the residents are serviced by the rural system which
allows the rural mail carrier to deliver mail to their boxes. Across the road, the residents must receive their mail through the box system.
One would think a matter like that could be easily cleared up. I have drawn it to the attention of the officials. However, that has not been the case. The situation has continued over the two or three years I have been making inquiries. I hope that with the new life this bill will breathe into the postal service by establishing the Canada Post Corporation, situations and difficulties of this kind will be remedied and that managers of our postal service will not feel they are bound by arrangements which have their base in historic facts no longer relevant to the current situation.
I mentioned the rural mail service. I want to speak briefly about the plight of our rural mail carriers. I said earlier, 1 respect the right of labour to organize and bargain collectively. I am mindful that there are 25,000 members represented by the Canadian Union of Postal Workers and 20,000 letter carriers represented by the Letter Carriers Union of Canada. 1 realize friction can develop between those groups and the rural mail carriers who do not have that kind of labour organization, although 1 understand they do have an association. However, they have in common the fact that they are all human beings, citizens of Canada who must earn their way.
The rural mail carriers, as most of us know, were placed in a very onerous position. When their contract expired and they wanted to renew it, they had to bid for the contract in common with everyone else who sought to supply the same service. This applied to contracts over $10,000-in this day and age, considering they have to supply a vehicle in all cases, that is not very much money. The result was that many rural mail carriers had to underbid in order to keep the service they were providing and which was their method of earning a livelihood. In many cases they suffered extreme financial losses.
This is a situation which should not have gone uncorrected for as long as it did. I understand that under the new legislation, it will not exist. I hope the step the government is proposing will result in more reasonable and rational treatment for our rural mail carriers.
In many rural parts of this country-I am sure my colleague for Parry Sound-Muskoka will verify this-residents are almost totally dependent on the mail service as their method of communication with friends and associates across this country and in other parts of the world. Because of the continuation, 1 hope, of six-day-a-week service, they are able to receive their daily newspapers and other periodicals. It is very important to their ability to communicate with their fellow Canadians and others across the world. We who serve rural constituencies are very much aware of the importance of this service. We hope it will be improved under this new bill. We certainly hope that some of the problems which existed in the past will be resolved.
There are one or two matters I would like to mention, but 1 am mindful of the clock, Mr. Speaker. I understand the minister will close the debate in a few minutes. I will just carry
November 20, 1980

on until the clock reaches the point at which the minister ought to have that opportunity. In the meantime 1 would like to mention a matter which is of serious and grave interest to many members, and of particular interest to myself. That is the provision in the bill-I believe it is clause 17-for the making of regulations. 1 sat for some days over the past months with a special committee on regulatory reform. Time and again business interests and labour interests-virtually the whole private sector-came before it to complain that the Government of Canada and in some cases provincial governments were abusing the power to make regulations. Statutes of the Parliament of Canada and of some of the provincial legislatures gave broad general powers to make regulations, so organizations and people in the private sector who were faced with the burden of those regulations simply did not know what the course and result of a particular statute would be.
We are disappointed to see that that kind of legislation has continued in Bill C-42 which, in clause 17, gives a very broad and extensive power to make regulations. I understand the minister has addressed himself to that point and will later on in this debate or at some appropriate time indicate the kinds of regulations which are likely to be enacted under that general authority. However, this should serve as a reminder to all of us who are concerned with regulatory reform and have an interest in removing or minimizing the burden on the private sector resulting from government regulation which in the end acts to the detriment of all Canadians and particularly consumers. Those of us who have an interest in that area would like to see a more general policy applied by the government in all legislation so that we could eliminate this abuse of the regulatory process. I am anxious to hear what the minister has to offer us in that connection so that the private sector can be assured that it will not suffer harm through the exercise of the regulatory authority granted by this bill.
By way of conclusion, let me say that the real purpose and hopefully the goal of this legislation is to improve postal service to customers, those who use the service-and in the circumstances this really amounts to all the people of Canada. If the postal service is not improved and if the charges applied to the services provided by the Post Office are not kept within reasonable limits, this whole exercise will have failed. The Crown corporation concept will have offered nothing in the way of improvement to postal service.
Let us remember-and 1 hope the minister is mindful of this-that all the utilization of the concept of a Crown corporation does, is give the postal service a new start. That new start has to involve better labour-management relations and the implementation and provision of a more effective postal service so that all Canadians will receive the benefits.

This bill which will change the department into a Crown corporation is eagerly awaited, need I say it again, not only by the officials of the Post Office Department but also by the representatives of the postal unions and their leaders. I firmly believe that the bill will considerably improve not only the postal administration but also the service and labour relations at the Post Office.
1 thank hon. members on both sides of the House who took part in the debate and most of all were willing to co-operate so that the bill will be given second reading tonight.
I listened carefully when my predecessor, the former Postmaster General, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), stated that as Postmaster General he would have liked to pilot this bill and have it passed by Parliament.
This is only the beginning. Today is November 20. 1 am aware that the postal unions would like this bill to be passed before the end of the year. 1 hope I can expect the same support from hon. members from both the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party, so that we can work together within the committee and arrive at the necessary amendments quickly. 1 say here and now that some of these amendments have been suggested by hon. members from the Progressive Conservative Party as well as the New Democratic Party, and it is with this attitude of openmindedness and co-operation that I will get down to work with the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, chaired by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), which will have to scrutinize every section of the bill and, should the need arise, approve the necessary amendments.
The committee, I know, is to get to work as early as next week. I hope it can report back before the middle of December, let us say, one month from now, so that this bill may come for third reading before Parliament. I do not want to exert any pressure on my hon. colleagues, make it an obligation for them
or anything, but I should like this bill to be studied, reported on and passed on third reading before Christmas.
In closing, I echo the comments made tonight by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) on the advisability of submitting some of the provisions of this bill to a joint committee of the House and the Senate with a view to their looking into certains aspects of the bill, especially the regulations. That committee shall not, of course, be authorized to amend the act. The only committee that can do so is the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates but I feel that the discussions, recommendations and suggestions of the joint committee of the House and the Senate, the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, can certainly be useful. In that spirit of co-operation, I thank all hon. members, not only on my own behalf, but also on behalf of all the Post Office employees who, I trust, are about to make up one of the nice corporations of Canada.

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINES-EXTENSION OF NATURAL GAS PIPELINE TO MARITIMES
NORTHERN PIPELINES-EXTENSION OF NATURAL GAS PIPELINE TO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29, 1980, I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in the House whether he can ensure that the government will be taking the necessary steps to provide for the extension of the natural gas pipeline eastward to Nova Scotia.
The minister, in response to my question, assured members of the House that the government would indeed take the necessary steps to ensure the construction of a pipeline to the east coast and to Nova Scotia. I had reason to question the minister and the Government of Canada on this matter because in January of 1980 the man who is now the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) appeared in Nova Scotia, in fact in my constituency, and stated in very clear terms that if he were elected, his Liberal government would take immediate action to ensure the full co-operation of all parties in the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes. That was not the Prime Minister's final word on the subject. In the Speech from the Throne the promise was repeated, and again in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on October 28 we heard the same promise.
We in Nova Scotia were well aware that the National Energy Board of Canada had denied the applicant permission to construct a gas pipeline to the east coast. The applicant in that case was Q & M Pipeline Limited which was later joined by TransCanada Pipelines Limited in the joint venture for the construction of the pipeline. The province of Nova Scotia appealed the decision of the National Energy Board to deny Q & M permission to construct the pipeline, and on the very day the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) had confirmed the government's intention to construct the pipeline, the National Energy Board dismissed the appeal.
So I ask the minister how he can guarantee to residents of the east coast that the National Energy Board will now, following the statement of government intention, approve the construction of a gas pipeline to the east coast.
Let me review briefly what is involved in obtaining the permission of the National Energy Board to construct a gas pipeline in Canada. An applicant must apply to the board for a certificate of public convenience. The procedure by which an applicant seeks such a certificate is very time consuming. Indeed, in many cases in the past it has taken not a matter of months, but years. I am told that an application of the kind required for the construction of a pipeline extension to the east
Adjournment Debate
coast could not even be under way until January, 1981, and even then it could take several months more before the National Energy Board could render its decision.
This does not appear to be consistent with another of the pronouncements of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources which was that a gas pipeline would be in place by 1983. It is difficult for some of us to understand how the minister could make such an undertaking when he could not even assure this House, or anyone else in any other forum, that an application would be under way before 1981 and speedily dealt with so as to allow construction to start in 1981. Most people familiar with pipeline construction could not imagine the construction work could be completed in less than two or three years. So we in the east are very suspicious that the minister is not telling us the entire facts and truth when he undertakes to have the pipeline in place by 1983.
This link from the east coast to the western gas supplies is vital to the future of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces which are now totally dependent upon foreign oil for much of their electrical generation and for the heating of their homes, not to mention transportation fuels which are absolutely essential to their economy. Not only is the pipeline linked to our energy supply, but it is an important factor in the development of a liquid natural gas terminal which we hope will be located in Nova Scotia on the Strait of Canso. In fact, proponents of that scheme, which include Petro-Canada, indicated that unless the pipeline is assured to the east coast, the liquid natural gas terminal, which would be part of the Arctic pilot project, would be located on the St. Lawrence River at Gros Cacouna. So, we see competition arising for the construction and location of the liquid natural gas terminal, and if the Strait of Canso is not in the running for that mammoth facility it will be because the National Energy Board failed to give permission to construct the gas pipeline extension.
On bringing these matters to the attention of the House and by raising the question with the minister, I received his firm undertaking that the government would indeed proceed with the construction of the natural gas pipeline extension. In fact, the minister indicated that if the National Energy Board did not provide speedy permission and grant a certificate as required under the legislation, he would present the House of Commons with a bill to implement construction.
I have before me the famous bill of 1956 which was an act to establish the Northern Ontario Pipeline Crown Corporation which, as all members know, caused a tremendous controversy. I hope the minister will not create a similar situation so that we will again be dependent upon the action of the government in bringing a bill before the House to implement the construction of the pipeline extension. I hope the minister will urge the National Energy Board to take speedy action and grant a certificate so that the pipeline can be completed on schedule in 1983.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINES-EXTENSION OF NATURAL GAS PIPELINE TO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question raised by the hon. member for Elalifax West (Mr. Crosby) on October 29 concerning the extension of the gas pipeline to the maritimes, I am pleased to remind the House of the assurance given by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) that this project is one of national priority. It is a matter to which the government attaches the highest importance.
In the Speech from the Throne in April of this year it was clearly stated that the federal government favours the earliest possible construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the Maritimes. The National Energy Board approved the extension to Quebec City. Although the board denied the application for the extension of the pipeline to the maritimes pending clarification of environmental specifications and east coast offshore gas development scheduling, the minister assured the House that the board would deal expeditiously with a new application. He gave a further undertaking that as a matter of national policy, the pipeline would be extended without delay, to be completed by 1983.
The National Energy Program, tabled on October 28, gives additional assurances. In the program, the federal government clearly stated that it supports construction of a gas pipeline to the maritimes. To ensure its financial feasibility, the government has initiated the following measures:
1.	The city-gate price of natural gas in maritime communities will be the same as Toronto.
2.	A contingency fund of up to $500 million will be available to assist in financing the pipeline if it is necessary.
3.	Grants of up to $800 will be available to consumers converting from oil heating to gas heating.
4.	Grants will be available to distribution companies to assist them to develop gas markets.
The National Energy Board has stated its willingness to deal expeditiously with a new application from the Trans Quebec and Maritime Pipeline sponsors. In turn, the company has indicated to the board that it is prepared to renew its application. A decision during the spring of 1981 would mean the pipeline could be delivering gas to Halifax by late 1983 and to Cape Breton by 1984.
in summary, Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear from the statement made in the Speech from the Throne last April regarding the extension of the natural gas pipeline to the maritimes, from the specific provisions relative to this project in the National Energy Program, and from the assurance given by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in the House on October 29, that natural gas services will be extended to the maritimes by 1983.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FINANCE-CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
FINANCE-CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 3 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-
Eachen) if he was considering an increase in the Canada Savings Bonds rate. At that time the Canada Savings Bonds program contemplated a rate of I0l/t per cent. I suggested 11 Vi per cent. Later that day-though the minister did not give me a commitment in this House that he would do it-he increased the rate on Canada Savings Bonds for this year to 11 Vi per cent.
This is not the first time that a government faced with massive redemptions and unsaleable Canada Savings Bonds in a sales program because of rapid changing interest factors has been forced to change the interest rate for one or two years or for the duration of a bond issue. The Hon. John Turner had to do it. My hon. friend from St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) had to do it. This minister has had to do it. It has happened many times before.
Canada Savings Bonds represent a very large demand on the debt structure of the country, although certainly not the demand they once did.
I remind the House that there were outstanding as of November 12, 1980, $15,681 billion of Canada Savings Bonds. At that time the program for the sale of these bonds was still under way for the current sale period.
I also remind the House that the redemption rate has been enormous. In times when interest rates rise very rapidly there is a tendency by people holding Canada Savings Bonds to cash their bonds and put their money into some better investment, some higher paying investment. So in a sense the government is blackmailed into a position where it must increase the interest payable on all its bond in order to slow down redemptions.
On a number of occasions in committee we have asked the government about the cost of the Canada Savings Bonds program. This program costs the Government of Canada about 1.25 per cent to sell the bonds.
I might point out these bonds are cashable on demand at any time. They are probably, in one sense of the word, one of the safest cash investments which a person could ever hope to acquire. However, with the problem of continual redemption, the cost of placing the bonds presents an enormous burden to the treasury. Guaranteed investment certificates are sold with a commission rate of one-fifth of 1 per cent, so that a trust company when borrowing on a five-year certificate, closed for five years, can borrow its money with a 1 per cent commission.
Yet, the government cost on commissions alone is 1 per cent, and with the other costs it comes to about 1.25 per cent. So the government is in a situation where the cost of borrowing money through Canada Saving Bonds is really not cheap. What it must do, therefore, is come up with another method of selling its Canada Savings Bonds.
I would like to offer a couple of suggestions. First, it might contemplate selling a 2 per cent bond plus inflation. Throughout the last century the British government financed itself on what were called British consuls. People received only 2 per
November 20, 1980

cent on the bonds because there was no inflation. People were happy with that rate of interest, which over time has been the safe rate of return which investors want on their money. The reason investors want 12 per cent, 13 per cent, or 14 per cent today is because of our rate of inflation. Investors want 2 per cent plus the rate of inflation.
Perhaps the government would find it much more attractive to sell an inflation-proof bond. By financing in this way, it would save itself a great deal of money on redemptions.
The second thing which the government might consider is a bond which has a flat rate of interest, say, 8 per cent, plus an adjusting rate of interest which floats up or down based on the average half-yearly rate on 90-day treasury bills.
I say this seriously to the government because unless it comes up with another program I shall be raising these points in the House during question period, perhaps next week, because, as we learned earlier, the 90-day rate on treasury bills at the option this afternoon was 13.06 per cent. The rate on the 180-day bills was another 30 basis points higher. Interest rates have risen virtually one full per cent since I raised this question with the minister on November 3. What will happen is the same thing as has happened before and it happens again and again. We will see a run on Canada Savings Bonds. People will cash their bonds and buy a better, higher-paying investment because they want a better return for their money.
If interest rates continue to rise, the minister will have to pay that extra point and make the return on the bond 12 per cent or 12.5 per cent. This is a continuous problem, and if the minister does not raise the return, then there will be redemptions and if there are redemptions, the minister will have to pay to the big boys-the banks and people dealing in treasury bills and bonds-the 13 per cent, 13.5 per cent or 14 per cent that will be required by the marketplace.
The ministry must come up with another system because people in Canada, strangely enough, want to lend money to the government. But they still want a fair return on their savings. Canadians do not want to wind up in the situation where they are receiving perceptively less than market rates for their money. The government must come up with a proposition which gives people a rate of return on their savings bonds that is related to the treasury bill rate or, if you like, to the Bank of Canada rate. Even if it is .5 per cent less than the Bank of Canada rate, then that would be fair, something which would be acceptable and which would save the government a great deal of money.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: FINANCE-CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-INQUIRY WHETHER INTEREST RATE WILL BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the question asked of the Minister of Finance on November 3 by the hon. member in which he suggested the CSB rate be reviewed at an early date. In fact, the minister announced at the same time that the rate of interest on the 1980-81 series for the year beginning November 1, 1980, would be raised to 11.5 per cent from 10.5 per cent. Further, the rate for the 1980-1981 year on all outstand-
Adjournment Debate
ing issues was increased by a full one percentage point to 11.5 per cent. This enhancement to the yield on CSBs largely offsets the increases in the rates which have taken place on short-term savings instruments since the terms of the new series were announced on September 12. The rates of return now payable on all outstanding issues of CSBs and the new series are attractive relative to competing savings instruments, given the other attractive features of the Canada Savings Bonds.
The 11.5 per cent first year CSB rate and 10.5 per cent rate payable in the remaining six years are somewhat lower than the current interest rates on other forms of government debt. For example, treasury bills for 91 and 182-day terms as at November 13 were yielding 12.42 per cent and 12.79 per cent respectively. Short, mid and long-term Canada bonds are presently yielding about 13 per cent. However, it is not unusual for CSBs to have a slightly lower rate of return than other forms of government debt. CSBs compete in a different market than this form of debt. The CSB rate is guaranteed for a full seven-year term on the new issue whereas treasury bill rates, while attractive at this moment, may well move down sharply when these short-term instruments mature. Government of Canada marketable bonds pay a higher rate of interest relative to CSBs due to the market risks associated with such instruments. If interest rates move to higher levels, investors will suffer a capital loss when selling Canada marketable bonds, whereas CSBs can always be redeemed at full face value. Another reason CSBs have a lower yield is that they are a more expensive form of financing relative to treasury bills and marketable bonds due to the issuing fees and commission structure. It is generally more expensive for the government to issue its debt in small denominations to a widely dispersed market, and these cost considerations are given careful consideration when determining the CSB rate. Consequently, the rate is set with a view to being as generous as possible for investors while at the same time minimizing as far as possible the public debt charges.
It has been suggested that the CSB rate should be equal to, or better than, the rate of inflation. The new 11.5 per cent first year CSB rate is higher than the inflation rate projection mentioned in the budget. I cannot say that the CSB rate will always be higher than the inflation rate at any point in time. In the past, it has not been unusual to experience periods when the rate of interest on most types of savings instruments has been below the rate of inflation. Such a phenomenon reflects investor expectations of lower inflation rates in the future. In the case of CSBs, investors over the past several years have generally enjoyed rates of return higher than the inflation rate. More important, the CSB rates, which have been increased periodically, have been quite attractive relative to rates of interest on short-term competing savings instruments.

ing tests of chemicals by a laboratory called IBT in the United States that were shown to be invalid. I was most surprised at the minister's response because the minister has a reputation of being one of the most progressive members of Cabinet and a person who is relatively sensitive to human and ecological issues. Her response seemed to indicate to me that we were touching on a very raw nerve.
I asked questions concerning chemicals, the IBT affair and the number of pesticides which are loose on the market today. Hundreds of millions of gallons of these products are used over a very large area yet we have found there exist no valid studies which tell us that the extended use of these products will not be harmful to human health, will not cause cancer or damage the reproductive process.
There are hundreds of new chemicals entering the human environment every year. The human chemical environment or world chemical environment has been greatly changed in the last decade or so, but unfortunately we find that the government has an attitude more appropriate to two decades ago. It certainly does not have the tools to deal adequately with this new phenomenon, this radical change in the environment. What we have found in the IBT case is that 99 per cent of the long-term studies were flawed. They were not accurate.
There is a fungicide called Captan. Thirteen of the 14 tests on that are invalid. We understand there are no other studies in existence to show that the fungicide Captan is not dangerous to human health. This product is used in very large quantities in the agricultural sector of this country, yet there are no studies which allow us to believe it is not harmful to human health.
In the past we have experienced some major crises. We all remember the case of thalidomide and the very unfortunate effects of that. There is no assurance that Captan is not like thalidomide, only stretched over a larger space of time. There are no valid studies. Captan is not the only one. IBT has done hundreds of studies. The American Environmental Protection Agency is now telling us that most of those studies were flawed. This is the type of information we have been trying to get from the government. I am not the only one. When the minister tells the House she has been most open with the public and her colleagues in the provinces, the record shows that this is not so, I wish to quote from the August 28, 1980, Leader-Post. It quotes the environment minister Ted Bower-man. I quote:
"Continued use of the chemicals in question with no public statement as to the particular flaws in the testing is an unsatisfactory position," Bowerman said.
"1 am anxious to learn of plans for improving the federal registration procedure and the development of a Canadian capability for conducting tests."
Mr. Bowerman has been asking questions of the department as to how many and what chemicals are involved. He has been asking for details of the chemicals with regard to which studies have been flawed, and for descriptions of the chemicals which were subject to valid studies. The government has consistently refused to let this information be made public. We have to go
to the United States to get the answer. I challenge the government to change its attitude where it relates to chemicals and the testing of chemicals, and to be open with the public.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to some of the allegations made by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). In a few moments I will provide him with a very technical answer. However, I wish to reply to some of the remarks he made with regard to the minister's involvement and the answers she gave in this House.
Over a period of time the hon. member for Regina East has been making these allegations in the House. The minister, to the best of her ability, has been giving the responses she is capable of giving at the present time. We in the department have made several attempts and have had individual meetings with the member involved to explain this to him.
I understand that the head of our health protection branch had a three-hour meeting with the hon. member to explain to him some of the data which is available to the department and the difficulties which arise from some of the data which have come from IBT, but to suggest that the health protection branch is not at least aware of the problem and doing the best it can with respect to the protection of health and the environment in Canada is a stretch of the imagination.
Approximately three years ago it was discovered that there were irregularities in certain animal studies conducted by IBT, a U.S. firm which conducts safety evaluations on behalf of pesticide manufacturers for submissin to U.S. and Canadian regulatory agencies. I think it is a fact well known to the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) that once such data was made available with that kind of irregularity a moratorium was placed on any product on which studies were done by IBT. Since that time we no longer accept the results of studies submitted by IBT to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as well as to our health protection branch. We no longer accept those results from that particular laboratory. This has forced the manufacturers in those cases where it was found that the tests were invalid to go back, at their own cost, to re-do the studies. I think it is well known that such a process takes considerable time.
Officers of the health protection branch working co-operatively with their counterparts in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency have determined that the status of approximately 100 pesticides depends on the validity of critical studies required to ensure that any potential human health risk is minimal. Additional IBT studies which were not pivotal to the original regulatory decision are also being reassessed, as time permits, in order to detect any undisclosed adverse effects. This reassessment may identify other chemicals of concern to those responsible for the safety of spray operators, wildlife, the environment, forest spraying, etc. The current list issued by the Environmental Protection Agency contains approximately twice as many pesticides as the Canadian list. The difference in the two lists is due to two facts. First, the Environmental
November 20, 1980

Protection Agency identified all studies for audit and validation while Canada identified only the critical studies for audit at this time. In other words, Canada identified key pivotal studies upon which a decision to register or not to register a pesticide rested. Second, some pesticides registered in the U.S. for uses such as on cotton are not required in Canada.
1 want to finish this because the hon. member asked for these figures on a previous occasion. As of October 1 of this year, 920 IBT studies have been identified in submissions from pesticide manufacturers. Of these, 247 are valid, 296 are adjudged invalid and 377 have not been audited to date.
